database-systems-map.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) data-modeling decision you face and draw its Database Systems Map: the storage engines in play, the directed write/read/index/replication flow between them, the suspect edge where integrity or freshness can break, and the system class you choose to model in — then start the artifact that carries the rest of this course.
database-systems-map.proof: Section 1 of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: a directed map of the relevant storage systems (OLTP store, replica, index/cache, analytics sink), the suspect edge marked, the system class chosen with the constraint that forced it, and an explicit out-of-scope boundary. A reviewer traces a single write from commit to query-visible without you narrating.
database-systems-map.unlock: Your map shows directed flow across at least three real storage systems, marks the suspect edge, names the system class you chose and why, and draws a defended scope boundary.
database-systems-map.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a systems map if you only named 'a database'. 'We use Postgres' is a product, not a map. The skill is showing where the truth lives, where copies of it lag, and which edge can serve a stale or inconsistent answer under load.

database-systems-map.text: A design review: the team wants to add a leaderboard query, someone says 'just put it in the database,' and the staff engineer asks one question - 'which database, and is it allowed to be five minutes stale?' The room stalls, because nobody mapped where the data actually lives versus where it gets read.

Every data model lives inside a system of stores - a source-of-truth OLTP engine, its replicas, an index or cache, an analytics sink - each with different consistency, isolation, and freshness guarantees. The Systems Map is the smallest accurate picture of those stores and the flow between them, and it is Section 1 of the migration-and-rollback packet you carry through this whole course.

database-systems-map.prompt: 'Let's just store it in Postgres.' Before you agree - what has that sentence already silently decided about your data? Answer before reading on.
database-systems-map.reveal: It pre-decided three things you have not earned: that you need ACID transactions (not just eventual consistency), that a single relational engine can serve both your writes AND your read patterns, and that the truth and the read copy are the same place. The real frame is a system class question: 'writes need a transactional source of truth with strong constraints, BUT the leaderboard read is high-fan-out and tolerates 60s staleness - so the truth lives in an OLTP store and the read is served from a derived index that lags.' Naming the product first feels decisive while quietly choosing the consistency model for you.

database-systems-map.intro: Writing Section 1, one line at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
database-systems-map.code:
## 1. Database Systems Map
[App] --write (txn)--> [Postgres Primary]  (source of truth: ACID, constraints, isolation)
                            |--streams WAL--> [Read Replica]   (async, lags ~seconds)
                            |--CDC index----> [Search Index]   (derived, eventually consistent)
                            |--nightly ETL--> [Warehouse]      (columnar, analytics only)
[App] --catalog query------------------------> [Search Index]  (reads here, NOT the primary)
- System class chosen: OLTP relational for the truth (needs constraints + multi-row transactions)
- Forced by constraint: order writes must be atomic and referentially valid; cannot lose a paid order
- Suspect edge: Primary -> CDC -> Search Index (freshness gap; a new product is query-invisible until indexed)
- Blast radius if it fails: search shows a stale catalog; conversions drop; NO data loss (truth intact in primary)
- Boundary we will NOT cross: the analytics warehouse path is out of scope for this decision
steps: The source of truth: Pick the engine that holds truth and the guarantees it owes you: ACID transactions, constraints, isolation. This is the one store a write is not 'done' until it commits to.
The derived copies: Replica and Search Index are COPIES, not truth. Mark them async - this is where lag and stale reads hide. A read served here can be seconds-to-minutes behind the primary.
The analytics sink: Columnar warehouse, batch-loaded. Different system class (column store, not row store) because the query pattern is aggregate scans, not point lookups.
The read path: The App queries the Search Index, NOT the primary. Whoever forgets this ships a feature that reads stale data and calls it a bug later.

System class + the constraint that forced it: State the class (OLTP relational) and the non-negotiable that ruled out alternatives: atomic, referentially-valid order writes rule out a plain key-value store as the truth.
Suspect edge + blast radius: The freshness gap lives on Primary -> CDC -> Search. Name that stale-catalog is recoverable (truth is intact) - stale is not lost, and that distinction sets urgency.
The boundary: Warehouse is out of scope - and you can defend why: nothing on the user-facing read path touches it.

storyboard.say: The app writes catalog changes into Postgres Primary, the one source of truth every other store copies from.
Postgres streams its write-ahead log to a read replica, giving you a scale-out copy for read traffic.
A nightly ETL job also loads Postgres into the columnar warehouse, sized for analytics, not live reads.
Change data capture feeds the search index, but this edge lags - the index trails the source of truth.
Yet the app queries that lagging search index directly, so users can read catalog data that is already stale.
So 'just put it in the database' is meaningless - the real question is which store, and how stale it's allowed to be.

database-systems-map.text: The senior tell is naming guarantees, not products. 'Postgres' tells a reviewer nothing; 'a transactional source of truth with foreign-key constraints and read-committed isolation, fronted by an eventually-consistent search index' tells them exactly what can break and where. A sound design principle is choosing the data model and consistency guarantees BEFORE the implementation - the map is how you make that choice visible and reviewable.

database-systems-map.question: What most distinguishes a useful Database Systems Map from naming your database product?
options: It uses an official diagramming tool instead of a whiteboard sketch.
It lists every microservice and table in the company so nothing is omitted.
It separates the source of truth from derived copies, shows directed flow, marks where freshness or integrity can break, and names the system class chosen with the constraint that forced it.
It records which team owns each database for the on-call rotation.
database-systems-map.explanation: Usefulness comes from showing guarantees and flow: which store holds truth (with its ACID/constraint/isolation guarantees), which stores are lagging copies, where a stale or inconsistent read can be served, and why the chosen system class fits the constraint. Completeness (2) reintroduces the clutter that hides the suspect edge; the tool (1) and ownership (4) are not the modeling decision.

database-systems-map.title: Find the products that are invisible to search because the CDC index hasn't caught up
database-systems-map.summary: Write one SQLite query (run it in the browser) that finds every product in the Postgres primary that has no row yet in the derived search index — the exact freshness-gap products a catalog search would fail to return.
database-systems-map.starter:
-- Database Systems Map: the CDC freshness gap
--
-- The store's SOURCE OF TRUTH is products_primary (the OLTP Postgres primary).
-- Every write lands here first, atomically.
--
-- The catalog page does NOT read the primary. It reads search_index, a DERIVED
-- store kept up to date by Change-Data-Capture (CDC). CDC is asynchronous, so a
-- brand-new product exists in the primary but is QUERY-INVISIBLE until it is
-- indexed. That lag is the "suspect edge" from the lesson.
--
-- products 3 and 5 were written to the primary but have not been indexed yet.

CREATE TABLE products_primary (
  product_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO products_primary (product_id, name, price_cents, created_at) VALUES
  (1, 'Cedar Desk',   24900, '2026-06-01T09:00:00Z'),
  (2, 'Oak Shelf',    13500, '2026-06-02T11:30:00Z'),
  (3, 'Maple Stool',   6900, '2026-06-03T08:15:00Z'),
  (4, 'Walnut Bench', 18800, '2026-06-04T14:45:00Z'),
  (5, 'Birch Lamp',    4200, '2026-06-05T10:05:00Z');

-- The derived, eventually-consistent read store the catalog actually queries.
CREATE TABLE search_index (
  product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  indexed_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO search_index (product_id, indexed_at) VALUES
  (1, '2026-06-01T09:00:07Z'),
  (2, '2026-06-02T11:30:05Z'),
  (4, '2026-06-04T14:45:09Z');

-- products_primary but is MISSING from search_index (the freshness-gap rows).
-- Return columns named product_id and name, ordered by product_id ascending.

entities-relationships.outcome: Take one real domain (orders, patients, courses — your pick) and model it as entities + relationships: name each entity and its primary key, draw the relationships with explicit cardinality, and enforce every relationship with a foreign-key constraint. Then package the change as schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md.
entities-relationships.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md containing: the entities + PKs, the relationships with cardinality, the FK constraints (DDL), the rejected denormalized option, the expected failure (an orphaned row), the verification method, and the rollback script. A reviewer can trace one row from child to parent and back without you narrating.
entities-relationships.unlock: Every relationship in your model is enforced by a foreign-key constraint with a named cardinality — no relationship lives only in your head or in application code.
entities-relationships.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'modeled the relationship' if the link exists only as a matching column name (orders.user_id with no FK). A column that happens to hold an id is not a relationship — the database does not know it is one, and it will let orphans in. The constraint IS the relationship.

entities-relationships.text: An order in production points at customer_id 8842. That customer was deleted last quarter. No FK was ever declared, so the database happily kept the orphan — and now the monthly revenue report sums orders whose customer no longer exists, and finance is asking why the numbers do not reconcile.

An entity is a thing you store rows about; a relationship is how two entities connect, and cardinality says how many. This is Section 1 of the schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md you carry through the rest of this course — schema, constraints, indexes, and migrations all stand on the entities and relationships you name here.

entities-relationships.prompt: An orders table has a customer_id column whose values match ids in the customers table. Is that a relationship the database will protect? Decide before reading on.
entities-relationships.reveal: No. Matching values are a convention, not a constraint. Until you declare FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id), the database treats customer_id as a plain integer — it will accept an order for a customer that never existed and let you delete a customer that still has orders. The relationship only becomes real, and only stays true under bad input, when a foreign-key constraint enforces it. The invariant of relational modeling: every reference points at a row that exists.

entities-relationships.intro: The schema for the model, one constraint at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: The parent entity + its primary key: customers is an entity: one row per real customer. The PRIMARY KEY id is what every relationship will point at — pick a stable surrogate key, not email, which can change.

The one-to-many relationship: customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) IS the relationship. NOT NULL makes it mandatory (every order has a customer); the FK makes it real (every customer_id points at a row that exists).

Cardinality via ON DELETE behavior: ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks deleting a customer who still has orders — the database refuses the orphan at the source. This is the rule the mission's broken system never had.

The many-to-many, resolved by a join entity: An order has many products and a product is on many orders. You cannot store that with one FK — order_items is the join entity, two FKs plus a composite PK so the same product cannot be added to an order twice.

CASCADE vs RESTRICT is a modeling decision: ON DELETE CASCADE on order_id: deleting an order removes its items (they cannot exist without it). RESTRICT on product_id: you must not delete a product still on live orders. Same syntax, opposite intent — chosen per relationship.
Index the foreign key: A FK is not auto-indexed in Postgres. Without idx_orders_customer, 'all orders for this customer' scans the whole table and the query plan degrades as orders grow.
entities-relationships.commonMistake: Integrity is a hope, not a guarantee

entities-relationships.title: A relationship is a foreign key with a cardinality, not a matching column
entities-relationships.text: An entity has a primary key. A relationship is a foreign key on the child pointing at the parent's primary key, with a stated cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-many). The invariant: no foreign key may reference a row that does not exist — that is referential integrity, and the constraint enforces it.

storyboard.say: Four entities live on the order path. Each stores rows about one kind of thing, and a primary key names each row uniquely.
A customer places many orders. That one-to-many link is a foreign key on Order pointing back at the customer's primary key.
An order splits into many line items, and each product appears across many line items. OrderItem is the join table resolving that many-to-many.
Here is the suspect edge. Order references a customer, but no foreign key was ever declared to enforce it.
Customer 8842 was deleted last quarter. With no constraint, the database kept the order pointing at a customer that no longer exists.
Now the revenue report sums orphaned orders, and finance cannot reconcile the numbers against real customers.
The invariant is referential integrity: no foreign key may point at a row that does not exist. A declared constraint enforces it.

steps.note: ON DELETE CASCADE on order_id: deleting an order removes its items (they cannot exist without it). RESTRICT on product_id: you must not delete a product still on live orders. Same syntax, opposite intent — chosen per relationship.

steps.label: Index the foreign key
steps.note: A FK is not auto-indexed in Postgres. Without idx_orders_customer, 'all orders for this customer' scans the whole table and the query plan degrades as orders grow.

entities-relationships.text: The senior tell: they decide ON DELETE behavior per relationship before writing the FK, because it encodes meaning. CASCADE says 'this child cannot exist without its parent' (order items); RESTRICT says 'this parent is referenced, refuse to orphan it' (a product on live orders); SET NULL says 'the link is optional, keep the row.' Grounded in the relational integrity rules of the SQL standard, the constraint is where the domain rule lives — not in a code comment.

entities-relationships.question: You need to model that an order contains many products and a product appears on many orders. What is the correct relational structure?
options: Add a products TEXT column on orders and store a comma-separated list of product ids.
Add an order_id column on products so each product points back to its order.
Create a join entity (e.g. order_items) with a foreign key to orders and a foreign key to products, and a composite primary key.
Add a product_id column on orders; if an order has several products, insert duplicate order rows.
entities-relationships.explanation: A many-to-many relationship cannot be expressed by a single foreign key on either side — that only models one-to-many. You resolve it with a join entity carrying one FK to each parent and a composite PK that prevents duplicate pairings. Option 1 destroys referential integrity (you cannot FK a comma-list); option 2 forces a product into exactly one order; option 4 duplicates the order entity and corrupts its identity.

normalization-denormalization.outcome: Take one schema that must change (or a realistic one) and write the decision packet: state whether you normalize to 3NF or deliberately denormalize a read path, name the integrity constraint you refuse to lose, the rejected option, and the rollback that restores truth if the migration goes wrong.
normalization-denormalization.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the selected normal form (or the named denormalization + its sync mechanism), the constraint that protects the invariant, the rejected approach, a DDL diff, and a rollback script. A reviewer reads it and can name what breaks if a duplicated field drifts.
normalization-denormalization.unlock: Your packet names the normal form, the constraint that guards the invariant, the rejected option, and a rollback that restores a single source of truth.
normalization-denormalization.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'denormalized for performance' if you never measured the query plan it was meant to fix and never wrote the mechanism that keeps the duplicated data in sync. A copied column with no sync rule is not an optimization — it is an update anomaly waiting for production.

normalization-denormalization.text: A customer's old address ships their refund to a house they moved out of two years ago — because the orders table stored a copy of the address that was never updated when they changed it. One duplicated column, one update anomaly, one very real package at the wrong door.

Normalization decides where each fact lives once; denormalization decides where you knowingly duplicate it to make a read fast. Get the boundary wrong and the database stops telling the truth under change — which is the one job the schema you carry through this course must never fail.

normalization-denormalization.prompt: An orders table stores customer_email in every row so reports don't need a join. A customer changes their email. What just happened to your data? Answer before reading on.
normalization-denormalization.reveal: You now have two versions of one fact and no rule saying which is true. That is an update anomaly: the email lives in two places, the UPDATE touched one, and every old order row still carries the stale value. The relationship 'a customer HAS an email' was supposed to live on the customer entity exactly once. Copying it felt faster until the day the copies disagreed — and a database whose copies disagree cannot answer 'what is this customer's email?' at all.

normalization-denormalization.intro: The DDL diff inside the decision packet. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: The redundant column: customer_email copied into every order is the transitive dependency 3NF forbids: email depends on customer, not on order.
One transaction: Wrap the migration so a failure mid-flight rolls back atomically — isolation means readers never see a half-applied schema.
The foreign key IS the invariant: The FK constraint makes 'every order points at a real customer' a database law, not a hope. This is the integrity you refuse to lose.
Backfill before you drop: Reconcile any row where the canonical value is missing BEFORE deleting the copy. Drop first and you destroy the only truth for orphan rows.
Drop the duplicate: The redundant fact is gone; the email now lives in exactly one place. The anomaly is structurally impossible now.
Rollback restores from truth: If the migration must reverse, re-add the column and refill it from customers.email — the source of truth — never from a backup of the stale copies.

normalization-denormalization.title: Normalize so each fact lives once; denormalize only with a sync rule
normalization-denormalization.text: Normalization removes redundancy: every fact lives in exactly one place, enforced by keys and constraints, so an update can't create two truths. The invariant: one fact, one home. Denormalization breaks that on purpose for read speed — and is only legitimate when you attach the mechanism that keeps the copy in sync.

the join that recombines normalized facts

storyboard.say: It starts with a single edit: a customer changes their email, and the write lands on just one copy of that fact.
The email lived in two tables. You updated one; every other copy silently drifts out of date.
This is the update anomaly: the same fact, stored twice, now holds two different values at once.
Two reads, two answers. The database can no longer tell you which email is true.
The repair sends that same write down a different path: normalize the email onto its one owning entity.
The order no longer stores its own copy. It holds a foreign key, referencing the one place the email lives.
You join on read to reassemble the fact, and it is always current, because there is only one copy to update.
One fact, one home. That invariant is the whole point: an update can no longer create two truths.

normalization-denormalization.title: Denormalize blindly vs. denormalize with a contract
normalization-denormalization.subtitle: Same goal: make the dashboard's per-customer order-count query fast. Only one stays true under change.

left.label: Copied column, no sync rule
lines: Added customers.order_count, set once at write time
No trigger, no job, no constraint keeping it current
A refund deletes an order; the counter never decrements
Now two facts disagree: COUNT(*) vs the cached number
No query plan was ever measured to justify it
left.verdict: An update anomaly sold as an optimization

right.label: Measured + a sync mechanism
lines: Proved the join was slow with EXPLAIN on real volume
Denormalized order_count WITH a trigger on insert/delete
The trigger is the contract that keeps the copy true
Reconciliation job re-derives it nightly as a backstop
Documented: chosen, rejected (no-cache), reversal condition
right.verdict: A defensible trade: speed bought, truth kept

normalization-denormalization.caption: Denormalization is legitimate only when the duplicate carries a mechanism that keeps it in sync with its source — and you measured the query plan that made it worth the risk.

normalization-denormalization.text: The senior tell is not 'normalize everything' — it is 'normalize by default, denormalize on evidence.' The relational model starts from one-fact-one-home; a pro deviates only with a measured query plan AND a named sync rule, and writes both into the migration. 'It felt slow' is not evidence, and a copy with no sync rule is not a cache — it is a future incident.

normalization-denormalization.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your denormalization is safe, not just fast. Which response actually proves it?
options: "The dashboard feels snappier now, and the team is happy with it."

"Here is the EXPLAIN showing the join was the bottleneck, the trigger that keeps the duplicated count in sync on insert and delete, a reconciliation job as backstop, and the rollback that drops the column and re-derives from the source of truth."
"We denormalized because joins are always slow at scale."
"We added the column and a comment in the code telling people to keep it updated."
normalization-denormalization.explanation: Only option 2 shows the full contract: a measured query plan justifying the duplication, an enforced sync mechanism (trigger) so the copy cannot silently drift, a reconciliation backstop, and a rollback that restores from the single source of truth. The others are vibes ('feels snappier'), a myth ('joins are always slow'), or a hope ('a comment telling people to update it') — none of which survive a refund deleting a row.

constraints-invariants.text: Two services write to orders at the same millisecond; both pass the app's "is this email taken?" check, both insert, and now one customer has two accounts that billing will fight over for a year. The app validated. The database did not — so the truth quietly broke.

A constraint is an invariant the database itself refuses to violate — true after every INSERT, UPDATE, and concurrent transaction, with no cooperation from application code. This is Section: Constraints of the migration packet you carry into the database capstone.

constraints-invariants.prompt: Your app checks `if not email_exists(email): insert(user)` before every signup, and code review is strict. Is the "one account per email" rule safe? Decide before reading on.
constraints-invariants.reveal: No — it has a race. Two requests run `email_exists` at the same instant, both see "free," both insert. The check-then-act gap is invisible in single-threaded testing and fatal under load. The database does not have the gap: a UNIQUE constraint makes the second INSERT fail atomically, because the engine enforces it inside the same isolation boundary as the write. App code guards a door; a constraint welds it shut.

constraints-invariants.intro: Writing the constraints, one invariant at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: INV-1 — NOT NULL + UNIQUE: This is the race from the pretest, closed for good. UNIQUE is enforced by an index inside the write's isolation boundary, so the second concurrent INSERT fails with 23505 instead of duplicating the row.
INV-2 — CHECK keeps money honest: balance >= 0 is a per-row invariant. A withdrawal that would overdraw is rejected by the engine, not by a hopeful `if amount <= balance` in three different services.

INV-3 — FK = referential integrity: An order can't point at a deleted account. ON DELETE RESTRICT makes the database refuse to orphan rows; the relationship between the two entities is now a guarantee, not a convention.

INV-4 — EXCLUDE for overlap: The invariant app code can't express: 'no two bookings for the same room overlap in time.' An EXCLUDE constraint over a range type enforces it across all writers — the kind of rule a UNIQUE can't reach.
One transaction, all-or-nothing: Wrapping in BEGIN/COMMIT means the migration is atomic: if INV-4 fails to build, INV-1..3 roll back too. You never land in a half-enforced schema.

On the app-only path both inserts land — a duplicate row, two accounts billing will fight over for a year.

constraints-invariants.text: The senior tell: a constraint that's never been rolled back hasn't been proven. Before you ship ADD CONSTRAINT on a live table, write and run the DROP CONSTRAINT rollback in a dry-run first — and on a hot table add it `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` separately, so validation doesn't hold an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock while production waits. A hard-won maintenance lesson: an invariant you can't safely reverse is a liability, not a guarantee.

constraints-invariants.question: A reviewer says: "You added a UNIQUE constraint on `email` in one migration that runs ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT on a 40-million-row production table during peak traffic." What is the strongest objection?
options: UNIQUE constraints are slower than application-level checks, so this hurts read performance.
Building the unique index to validate 40M rows takes a long lock that blocks writes; split it — CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then attach it — and ship a tested rollback.
UNIQUE can't enforce one-account-per-email; only application code can do that correctly.
You should use a CHECK constraint instead of UNIQUE for email.
constraints-invariants.explanation: The invariant choice (UNIQUE) is right — option 3 inverts reality, since the constraint is exactly what closes the race app code can't. The real production failure is operational: validating 40M rows under a blocking lock stalls writes. The gold path builds the index CONCURRENTLY off the critical path, attaches it, and carries a tested rollback. Option 1 misframes correctness as a read-perf tradeoff; option 4 picks a constraint type that can't express uniqueness.

indexes-access-patterns.text: The orders page that loaded in 40ms for 10,000 rows now takes 9 seconds at 4 million — same query, same code, untouched. Someone added an index last quarter; the planner ignores it, because it was built for a column order no real query asks for.

An index is not decoration on a table; it is a data structure shaped for a specific access pattern. Pick the pattern wrong and you pay a write tax for a structure no read uses — this is Section 'Indexes & Access Patterns' of the migration packet you carry through the module.

indexes-access-patterns.prompt: Your query is WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. You add INDEX(created_at, tenant_id, status). It's still slow. Why — the columns are all there?
indexes-access-patterns.reveal: A B-tree is sorted left-to-right, so the FIRST column decides everything. Leading with created_at means the index is ordered by date across all tenants — to satisfy tenant_id = ? the planner must scan the whole tree. The rule is equality columns first, then the sort column, then ranges: INDEX(tenant_id, status, created_at). Now the equality predicates jump to a contiguous slice already ordered by created_at, so the LIMIT 20 reads 20 rows and stops — no sort, no scan.

indexes-access-patterns.intro: Designing the index from the query, then proving it. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
indexes-access-patterns.code:
-- ## Indexes & Access Patterns
-- Hot access pattern (the read we are serving):
SELECT id, total FROM orders
 WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'open'
 ORDER BY created_at DESC
 LIMIT 20;

-- Chosen index: equality (tenant_id, status) -> sort (created_at)
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_status_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);

-- Rejected: leading with the sort column
-- CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_tenant ON orders (created_at, tenant_id);
--   why rejected: created_at first => filter can't pin a slice => Seq Scan

-- Proof (run before and after the CREATE):
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total FROM orders
 WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'open'
 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Rollback:
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_status_created;
steps: Read the access pattern first: Equality columns: tenant_id, status. Sort column: created_at DESC. Bound: LIMIT 20. The index is designed FROM these four lines, never from the table definition.

Column order = equality, then sort: (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC): the two equality predicates pin a contiguous slice, and created_at DESC means that slice is already in the order the query wants — the LIMIT reads 20 and stops.

CONCURRENTLY = no write lock: On a live 4M-row table, a plain CREATE INDEX takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and blocks writes. CONCURRENTLY trades a slower build for zero downtime — a migration-safety call, not a performance one.

Name the rejected option: Leading with created_at is the seductive wrong answer: the column you sort by feels like it should come first. It can't pin the equality slice, so the planner falls back to Seq Scan + Sort. Writing down why you rejected it is the reviewable judgment.

EXPLAIN is the proof, not the vibe: Run it before and after. 'Seq Scan on orders ... rows=4000000' must become 'Index Scan using idx_orders_tenant_status_created ... rows=20' with the Sort node gone. No plan change = no proof.
Rollback ships with the change: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY is the reversal condition. An index migration without a written rollback is a one-way door pretending to be reversible.

storyboard.say: A query hits the orders page and lands at the planner — same code that returned 10,000 rows in 40ms now faces 4 million.
The planner's whole job is one choice: given this query, which index actually matches how it narrows and sorts?
Someone added idx(created_at, tenant_id) — but its leading column isn't how this query filters, so there's no usable left prefix.
With no matching prefix, the planner falls back to a full Seq Scan plus a Sort — the 9-second path.
The other index leads with the equality filter, then the ORDER BY column — a clean left-prefix match.
That match drives an Index Scan that walks a pre-sorted slice and stops at LIMIT — fetching just 20 rows.
The lesson: order composite columns equality-first, then ORDER BY, then range — the left prefix must match how the query reads.

indexes-access-patterns.text: The senior tell is reading EXPLAIN, not trusting CREATE INDEX. Every index is a standing write cost: each INSERT (and each UPDATE touching an indexed column) has to update every matching index, not just the table. So a pro deletes the indexes no query plan actually uses as fast as they add the one the hot path needs — an unused index is pure tax with no service.

indexes-access-patterns.question: For WHERE org_id = ? AND archived = false ORDER BY updated_at DESC, which composite index lets the planner skip the sort and avoid a full scan?
options: INDEX(updated_at, org_id, archived) — put the sort column first so results come out ordered.
INDEX(org_id, archived, updated_at) — equality columns first, then the ORDER BY column.
INDEX(org_id), INDEX(archived), INDEX(updated_at) — three single-column indexes so each predicate is covered.
INDEX(archived, org_id, updated_at) — the most selective-sounding column first.
indexes-access-patterns.explanation: Equality predicates (org_id, archived) must lead so the B-tree pins one contiguous slice; updated_at last means that slice is already ordered, so the planner reads it in reverse and skips the Sort. Leading with updated_at (1) can't pin the slice → Seq Scan. Three separate indexes (3) force a slower bitmap combine and still need a sort. Reordering equality columns (4) doesn't help the sort — and 'most selective first' is a single-column heuristic, not a composite-ordering rule.

query-design-joins.text: The finance dashboard shows $4.2M in revenue. The ledger shows $1.4M. Nobody touched the numbers — someone added a JOIN to orders → line_items and the SUM(order_total) quietly tripled, once per line item. The query ran green the whole time.

A JOIN is not 'glue between tables' — it changes the grain of your result set, the unit each row represents. Get the grain wrong and every COUNT, SUM, and AVG downstream is wrong while the query still succeeds. This is Section 2 of the migration packet you carry through the module.

query-design-joins.prompt: You join orders (1 row each) to line_items (3 rows each) and SELECT SUM(orders.total). One order, total = $100, has 3 line items. What does the SUM return — and why is that the trap? Answer before reading.
query-design-joins.reveal: It returns $300. The JOIN fans the single order row out to three rows (one per line item), so orders.total is repeated three times and summed three times. The query is valid SQL, the plan is optimal, the result is wrong by exactly the child cardinality. The grain silently shifted from 'one row per order' to 'one row per line item' — and your aggregate followed it.

query-design-joins.intro: The query, stepped — fan-out vs. pre-aggregated join. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
query-design-joins.code:
-- ✗ NAIVE: joins straight to line_items → fan-out
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total)      AS revenue,   -- triple-counted
       COUNT(li.id)            AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN line_items li ON li.order_id  = o.id   -- grain becomes 1 row / item
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- ✓ REPAIR: pre-aggregate line_items to ORDER grain, then join
WITH item_rollup AS (
  SELECT order_id,
         COUNT(*) AS item_count
  FROM line_items
  GROUP BY order_id                          -- 1 row / order, no fan-out
)
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total)        AS revenue,  -- counted once
       SUM(ir.item_count)        AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN item_rollup ir ON ir.order_id = o.id    -- grain stays 1 row / order
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- PROOF: revenue must equal the independent ledger total
SELECT SUM(order_total) AS truth FROM orders;  -- compare to query output
steps: The grain claim: This query intends 'one row per customer'. SUM(o.order_total) is only correct if each order row appears once — but the next line breaks that.
The fan-out edge: Joining line_items multiplies each order by its item count. The result grain is now 'one row per line item', and order_total is duplicated across them.
Pre-aggregate the child: The CTE collapses line_items to one row per order BEFORE the join. This is the move: fix the grain at the source, not after.
Join at parent grain: Now orders ⋈ item_rollup is 1:1 on order_id. order_total appears exactly once per order, so SUM is honest.
The proof query: An independent SUM(order_total) over orders alone is ground truth. If the joined revenue equals this, the grain held. If it is a multiple, you fanned out.

query-design-joins.title: A JOIN sets the grain; aggregate at the grain you mean
query-design-joins.text: Every join multiplies rows by the matched cardinality. A one-to-many join makes the parent's grain become the child's. The invariant: SUM/COUNT the parent only at the parent's grain — aggregate the child first, then join, or your totals inherit the fan-out.

query-design-joins.title: Where the fan-out happens — and the repair path
query-design-joins.subtitle: orders (grain: one row per order) joined to line_items (one row per item) fans 1 order → 3 rows. SUM(order_total) over that grain triple-counts. The repair: pre-aggregate line_items to order grain, THEN join.

legend.label: fan-out failure — grain shifted to the child
repair — pre-aggregate child to parent grain
correct grain, correct total

storyboard.say: Start here: one order and its line items. The dashboard reports $4.2M, but the ledger says $1.4M — and nobody touched the numbers.
Someone added a JOIN. One order row meets three line-item rows — that's a one-to-many relationship waiting to multiply.
The join changes the grain. One order becomes three rows in the result — the parent now inherits the child's grain.
Now SUM order_total runs over the fanned-out rows and triple-counts. That's the failure path — and the query still returns green.
The repair: roll line_items up to order grain first, so each order collapses back to a single row before it ever meets the parent.
Now join at order grain — one order row meets one pre-aggregated row per order. The fan-out never happens.
SUM order_total over the correct grain returns the true $1.4M. The invariant: aggregate the child first, then join.

query-design-joins.title: The query, stepped — fan-out vs. pre-aggregated join
query-design-joins.subtitle: Same question ('total revenue per customer, with item counts'), two grains. Only the second keeps SUM honest.
query-design-joins.code:
-- ✗ NAIVE: joins straight to line_items → fan-out
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total)      AS revenue,   -- triple-counted
       COUNT(li.id)            AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN line_items li ON li.order_id  = o.id   -- grain becomes 1 row / item
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- ✓ REPAIR: pre-aggregate line_items to ORDER grain, then join
WITH item_rollup AS (
  SELECT order_id,
         COUNT(*) AS item_count
  FROM line_items
  GROUP BY order_id                          -- 1 row / order, no fan-out
)
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total)        AS revenue,  -- counted once
       SUM(ir.item_count)        AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN item_rollup ir ON ir.order_id = o.id    -- grain stays 1 row / order
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- PROOF: revenue must equal the independent ledger total
SELECT SUM(order_total) AS truth FROM orders;  -- compare to query output

steps.label: The grain claim
steps.note: This query intends 'one row per customer'. SUM(o.order_total) is only correct if each order row appears once — but the next line breaks that.

steps.label: The fan-out edge
steps.note: Joining line_items multiplies each order by its item count. The result grain is now 'one row per line item', and order_total is duplicated across them.

steps.label: Pre-aggregate the child
steps.note: The CTE collapses line_items to one row per order BEFORE the join. This is the move: fix the grain at the source, not after.

steps.label: Join at parent grain
steps.note: Now orders ⋈ item_rollup is 1:1 on order_id. order_total appears exactly once per order, so SUM is honest.

steps.label: The proof query
steps.note: An independent SUM(order_total) over orders alone is ground truth. If the joined revenue equals this, the grain held. If it is a multiple, you fanned out.

query-design-joins.caption: Index note: ensure line_items(order_id) and orders(customer_id) are indexed — the planner picks a hash/merge join on them; without the index it falls to a nested loop that scans line_items per order.

query-design-joins.text: Senior reviewers read a JOIN by asking one question first: 'what is one row here?' If you cannot state the grain in a sentence, the SUM cannot be trusted. CS2023's Data Management knowledge area covers relational query design and data integrity; SWEBOK V4 has no query-design or database content. A fan-out join violates row-level integrity invisibly, which is exactly why it caps a lesson without a proof: the result is plausible, never verified.

query-design-joins.question: Your report joins invoices to a one-to-many payments table and SUM(invoice_amount) looks too high. What is the correct fix?
options: Add SELECT DISTINCT to remove duplicate rows before the SUM.
Pre-aggregate payments to the invoice grain (GROUP BY invoice_id) in a subquery/CTE, then join so each invoice row appears once.
Switch the INNER JOIN to a LEFT JOIN so no rows are dropped.
Add an index on payments.invoice_id so the SUM runs faster.
query-design-joins.explanation: The SUM is inflated because the one-to-many join fanned each invoice out across its payments, duplicating invoice_amount. Pre-aggregating payments to invoice grain restores a 1:1 join so invoice_amount is summed once. DISTINCT (1) collapses identical rows but silently drops legitimately-equal amounts and breaks COUNT; LEFT JOIN (3) changes which rows appear, not the fan-out; an index (4) makes the wrong number arrive faster.

transactions-atomicity.outcome: Take one realistic multi-statement write (a money transfer, an order + inventory decrement, a multi-table migration) and make it ATOMIC: wrap it in one transaction so it either fully commits or fully rolls back, then capture the decision in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md — context, the constraint you protect, the selected approach, the rejected approach, and the exact failure you fear.
transactions-atomicity.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md plus a transcript: run the multi-statement write, kill it mid-flight (raise an error between the two UPDATEs), and SELECT both rows afterward. A reviewer sees the database returned to its pre-transaction state — no half-applied write — and your packet names the invariant the transaction protected.
transactions-atomicity.unlock: Your write is wrapped in BEGIN/COMMIT with a ROLLBACK path, you demonstrated a mid-transaction failure leaving zero partial state, and your packet names the all-or-nothing invariant by which it was judged.
transactions-atomicity.doNotClaim: Do not claim atomicity because you wrote BEGIN. Atomicity is proven by the ABORT path, not the happy path. If you never showed a forced mid-transaction failure rolling everything back, you proved a successful insert, not an atomic unit of work.

transactions-atomicity.text: Account A is debited $500. Then — before the matching credit lands in Account B — the process is killed: a deploy, a deadlock, a network blip. The money has now simply evaporated, and the ledger that was supposed to hold the truth is the thing that lost it.

Real writes are rarely a single statement — a transfer is a debit AND a credit, an order is an insert AND an inventory decrement. Atomicity is the rule that fuses those statements into one indivisible unit: all of them commit, or none of them do, even when the process dies between them.

transactions-atomicity.prompt: You run two UPDATEs back-to-back with no transaction: debit A, then credit B. The first succeeds, then the connection drops before the second. What is the state of the database? Decide before reading on.
transactions-atomicity.reveal: Permanently half-applied: A is down $500, B is unchanged, and nothing will ever reconcile it — the debit already committed on its own. Without a transaction, each statement is its own atomic unit, so 'two statements' means 'two independent commits.' The fix is not more retries or careful ordering; it is declaring the two statements ONE unit with BEGIN/COMMIT, so the dropped connection rolls the debit back instead of leaving torn money in the ledger.

transactions-atomicity.intro: Making the transfer atomic — one transaction, proven by the abort. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: The weak version: No BEGIN means each UPDATE is its own atomic unit and commits independently. A failure after line 2 leaves the debit applied and the credit lost — torn money.
BEGIN / COMMIT fuse the statements: Everything between BEGIN and COMMIT is one unit of work. Until COMMIT runs, the writes are staged and reversible — not yet durable.

Defend the invariant inside the unit: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint evaluated mid-transaction aborts the whole transaction, not just the offending row — so a bad input can never leave a half-transfer.
Force the abort — this is the proof: SELECT 1/0 stands in for a real mid-flight failure. Postgres marks the transaction aborted; COMMIT can no longer succeed.
Inspect the result: Both rows are unchanged. The debit was rolled back with the credit it was never paired to. All-or-nothing resolved to NOTHING — exactly the guarantee.
transactions-atomicity.commonMistake: Torn money — the ledger lost the truth it stored

transactions-atomicity.title: Atomicity is all-or-nothing: the transaction is the indivisible unit
transactions-atomicity.text: A transaction groups statements so they commit together or abort together — there is no partial outcome. The invariant: at every point an observer can see, either all the writes happened or none did. A mid-flight failure must leave the database exactly as it was before BEGIN.

transactions-atomicity.title: The transfer as one atomic unit — commit path and abort path
transactions-atomicity.subtitle: BEGIN opens the unit; the debit and credit are staged inside it. A failure between them routes to ROLLBACK, restoring pre-transaction state. Only a clean COMMIT makes either write durable. The torn middle state is never observable.

legend.label: inside the transaction (staged, reversible)
COMMIT — every write becomes durable together
ROLLBACK — every write is discarded together

storyboard.say: A client asks to move $500 between accounts. That single request is really two writes, and it opens a transaction.
BEGIN wraps everything that follows into one unit. Stage one debits Account A by $500.
This is the danger point. Between the debit and the credit, the process could die from a deploy, deadlock, or network blip.
If a fault strikes here, we route to ROLLBACK, which restores the exact pre-transaction state as if BEGIN never happened.
With no fault, we proceed and stage the matching credit: Account B gains $500. Both writes are now staged but not yet durable.
Only a clean COMMIT makes both writes durable at once. This is the all-or-nothing gate.
The ledger ends in one of two honest states: ALL writes landed, or NONE did. The torn middle is never observable.

transactions-atomicity.text: Atomicity is the A in ACID: a transaction is the unit of recovery. (SWEBOK V4 has no 'data-management body of knowledge'; ACID/transaction concepts live in the ACM/IEEE CS2023 Data Management knowledge area, not SWEBOK.) The reviewer's lens is integrity under failure, not under success. Pair it with a CHECK constraint and you get two layers — the constraint refuses bad data, the transaction guarantees that refusal undoes the whole unit rather than half of it.

transactions-atomicity.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence that this transfer is atomic and not just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually proves it?
options: Point to the BEGIN and COMMIT keywords in the code and explain that they group the statements.
Run the transfer once, SELECT both balances, and show the money moved correctly.
Force a failure between the debit and the credit, then SELECT both rows and show neither was changed — the whole unit rolled back.
Show that the accounts table has a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint.
transactions-atomicity.explanation: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee under failure, so the only evidence that proves it is the abort path: a forced mid-transaction failure leaving ZERO partial state. Keywords (0) describe intent, the happy-path run (1) only shows a successful write, and the constraint (3) guards the value but does not by itself prove the debit rolls back with the failed credit.

transactions-atomicity.title: Make a money transfer atomic, then prove a rolled-back transfer leaves no trace
transactions-atomicity.summary: Wrap two account transfers in transactions — one you COMMIT and one you ROLLBACK — then run the script in the browser to prove that a rolled-back unit of work changes nothing, while a committed one persists in full.
transactions-atomicity.starter:
-- Bank ledger. The CHECK constraint is the invariant we must never break:
-- no account may ever go negative.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner   TEXT NOT NULL,
  balance INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, owner, balance) VALUES
  ('A', 'Ada',  300),
  ('B', 'Boaz', 120),
  ('C', 'Cyra', 900);

-- A transfer is a single ATOMIC unit of work: the debit and the credit
-- either BOTH happen or NEITHER does. Two loose UPDATEs are a bug — a crash
-- between them loses money. Wrap each transfer in BEGIN ... COMMIT/ROLLBACK.

-- ============================================================
-- TODO 1: Transfer 250 from Cyra ('C') to Ada ('A') as ONE atomic unit,
--         and COMMIT it so it persists.
--         (debit C by 250, credit A by 250, inside one transaction)


-- TODO 2: Start a transfer of 90 from Boaz ('B') to Cyra ('C'), but this
--         one gets cancelled: ROLLBACK the WHOLE unit so NEITHER row
--         changes. Because it is rolled back, it must leave zero trace.


-- ============================================================
-- Do not edit below. This inspects the final ledger.
SELECT id, owner, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
transactions-atomicity.check:
id | owner | balance
A | Ada | 550
B | Boaz | 120
C | Cyra | 650

isolation-concurrency.text: Two customers buy the last concert ticket within the same 40 milliseconds. Both transactions read inventory = 1, both subtract one, both COMMIT, and the table now reads inventory = 0 — but you sold two tickets to a single seat. No error fired. The lost update is invisible until the venue calls.

This lesson sits in the applied-skill phase of Databases and Data Modeling: you already model entities, constraints, and transactions, but a schema that is correct for one user can silently corrupt under concurrent ones. Isolation is the property that decides whether your invariants survive load — Section 4 of the migration-and-rollback packet you carry through this module.

isolation-concurrency.prompt: Two transactions both run BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 7; COMMIT at the same time. Is the final balance guaranteed correct? Decide before reading on.
isolation-concurrency.reveal: Yes — and that is the trap that teaches the wrong lesson. balance = balance + 100 is a single atomic UPDATE, so the database locks the row and serializes the two writes for you. But the moment you split it into a READ then a WRITE — SELECT balance (app adds 100) UPDATE balance = 600 — both transactions read 500, both write 600, and one +100 vanishes. The anomaly is not in the transaction; it is in the read-modify-write gap, and only the isolation level decides what happens inside that gap.

isolation-concurrency.code:
## 4. Isolation Decision
# Anomaly: lost update on inventory.qty (read-modify-write across app code)

# --- FAILURE: READ COMMITTED, two concurrent sessions ---
# Session A                          # Session B
BEGIN;                               BEGIN;
SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE id=7;  -- A reads 1
                                    SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE id=7;  -- B also reads 1
UPDATE inventory SET qty=0 WHERE id=7;
COMMIT;                             UPDATE inventory SET qty=0 WHERE id=7;  -- overwrites
                                    COMMIT;   -- qty=0, but TWO tickets sold

# --- REPAIR: take the row lock on read ---
BEGIN;
SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE id=7 FOR UPDATE;  -- A locks the row
                                    -- B's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE now BLOCKS here
UPDATE inventory SET qty=qty-1 WHERE id=7 AND qty>0;
COMMIT;                             -- B unblocks, re-reads qty=0, sells nothing

# Rejected: SERIALIZABLE globally -> correct but serialization_failure
# retries under load; FOR UPDATE scopes the cost to this one hot row.
steps: Name the anomaly first: Lost update on a read-modify-write — not 'concurrency bug'. The named anomaly is what the rest of the packet must close.
Both sessions read the same value: Under READ COMMITTED, B's SELECT sees the last committed value and does not block. Both read qty=1 — the gap is open.
Second write silently wins: A commits qty=0; B's UPDATE then overwrites with its own qty=0. No error — the database did exactly what each transaction asked.
FOR UPDATE locks on read: The repair: A's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a row-level write lock, so B's identical SELECT blocks instead of reading stale data.
Guarded decrement: qty=qty-1 ... AND qty>0 is the real decrement. When B unblocks it re-reads qty=0, the WHERE fails, and zero rows change — the oversell is refused.

Record the rejected option: SERIALIZABLE is correct but converts the race into serialization_failure errors the app must retry. FOR UPDATE pays the cost only on the hot row — that tradeoff is the reviewable judgment.

storyboard.say: Two customers buy the last ticket at once. T1 opens a transaction and reads the quantity, seeing exactly one in stock.
In the same instant, T2 also reads the row. Under READ COMMITTED it sees one too, because T1 hasn't committed yet.
T1 finishes its read-modify-write, subtracting one and writing quantity equals zero, then commits.
T2, still holding its stale read of one, does the same math and writes zero — overwriting T1's result blindly.
Both writes land on zero, but two tickets were sold to one seat. No error fired — this is the silent lost update.
The guard cuts it here: SELECT FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE makes T1's read acquire a lock on the row.
T2 can't read past the lock. It waits for T1 to commit, then re-reads quantity equals zero and is correctly refused.
The lesson: pick the weakest isolation or narrowest lock that still forbids the anomaly your invariant depends on.

isolation-concurrency.text: Standards grounding (ACM/IEEE CS2023, Data Management): the SQL standard's four isolation levels are defined by which phenomena they forbid, and most databases do not match the names. (SWEBOK V4 does not cover SQL isolation levels; drop it as an authority here.) PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED, its 'REPEATABLE READ' is actually snapshot isolation (which prevents lost updates but NOT write skew), and only SERIALIZABLE forbids write skew. Never reason from the level's name — reason from the anomaly it is documented to prevent on your engine.

isolation-concurrency.question: A reviewer asks: 'You set the transaction to REPEATABLE READ — does that make this transfer-between-accounts logic correct?' What is the right answer?
options: Yes — REPEATABLE READ is a high level, so all anomalies are prevented.

It prevents dirty reads and lost updates, but on Postgres's snapshot isolation it does NOT prevent write skew, so if the invariant spans two rows (e.g. 'both balances must stay >= 0') you still need SERIALIZABLE or an explicit lock.
No — only READ UNCOMMITTED is safe for transfers.
It does not matter, because BEGIN/COMMIT already makes it serializable.
isolation-concurrency.explanation: Write skew is the anomaly that survives snapshot isolation: two transactions each read a consistent snapshot, each check an invariant that holds, and each commit a change that — together — violate it. The classic case is two withdrawals that each see the combined balance as sufficient. REPEATABLE READ on Postgres is snapshot isolation and does not forbid it; SERIALIZABLE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the read set does. Options 1 and 4 confuse atomicity with serializability.

isolation-concurrency.starter:
-- Isolation & concurrency: hunting the lost-update anomaly
--
-- A lost update happens when two sessions each do read-modify-write on the
-- same row: they BOTH read the same starting qty, both subtract, and the
-- second COMMIT silently overwrites the first. The lesson's fix was to take
-- a row lock on read (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so the second session blocks.
--
-- This table is the post-mortem audit log. Each row is one committed
-- transaction: which item it touched, which session did it, the qty it READ
-- at BEGIN, and the qty it WROTE at COMMIT. The fingerprint of a lost update
-- is two or more committed writes to the SAME item that READ the SAME qty --
-- proof they ran against the same snapshot instead of being serialized.

CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  item_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  session      TEXT    NOT NULL,
  qty_read     INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- value the txn read at BEGIN
  qty_written  INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- value the txn wrote at COMMIT
  committed_at TEXT    NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO audit_log (id, item_id, session, qty_read, qty_written, committed_at) VALUES
  (1, 7,  'A', 5, 4, '2026-06-01T09:00:01'),  -- A reads 5
  (2, 7,  'B', 5, 4, '2026-06-01T09:00:02'),  -- B ALSO read 5 -> lost update
  (3, 12, 'A', 8, 7, '2026-06-01T09:05:00'),  -- read 8...
  (4, 12, 'A', 7, 6, '2026-06-01T09:05:03'),  -- then read 7: serialized, safe
  (5, 20, 'A', 3, 2, '2026-06-01T09:10:00'),  -- read 3...
  (6, 20, 'B', 2, 1, '2026-06-01T09:10:04'),  -- read 2: serialized, safe
  (7, 31, 'A', 9, 8, '2026-06-01T09:20:00'),  -- A reads 9
  (8, 31, 'B', 9, 8, '2026-06-01T09:20:01'),  -- B read 9
  (9, 31, 'C', 9, 8, '2026-06-01T09:20:02');  -- C read 9 -> three-way lost update

isolation-concurrency.intro: Prove the isolation decision holds — no hand-waving:
items: Name the exact anomaly (dirty read, lost update, write skew, or phantom). 'Concurrency bug' is not a name and cannot be tested.

migrations-schema-evolution.doNotClaim: Do not claim a migration is safe because it ran on your empty local dev table. An empty table passes every constraint and locks nothing. The proof is that it preserves the existing rows and acquires no long-held lock on a populated table under writes.

migrations-schema-evolution.text: 2 a.m. deploy: a one-line ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL takes a full table lock on 80 million rows, every checkout write blocks behind it, and the on-call watches the error rate go vertical for the eleven minutes it takes to rewrite the table. The column was trivial. The migration was the outage.

A schema is a contract that thousands of live rows and a running application already depend on; evolving it is changing the contract while both sides keep talking. This lesson turns 'I edited the schema' into a reviewable packet that preserves every existing row, locks nothing for long, and can be reversed — the artifact your database capstone reuses for every change.

migrations-schema-evolution.prompt: You need a new non-null column on a 50-million-row table. Two options: one ALTER that adds the column NOT NULL with a default in a single statement, or three smaller migrations. Which is safer — and why isn't the one-liner the obvious win? Decide before reading.
migrations-schema-evolution.reveal: The one-liner is a trap on older or strict engines: adding a NOT NULL column forces the database to verify or rewrite every existing row, taking a lock that blocks writes for the whole rewrite. The safe path is expand-contract: (1) add the column nullable (instant, metadata-only), (2) backfill in small batches with no global lock, (3) add the NOT NULL constraint as a separate, validatable step. Three migrations is slower to write and faster to ship safely — because none of them holds a long lock or strands a row.

migrations-schema-evolution.intro: The packet's forward + rollback DDL, step by step. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
migrations-schema-evolution.code:
-- == FORWARD (expand-contract) ==
-- Phase 1 expand: instant, metadata-only, fully reversible
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN contact_email text;          -- nullable on purpose

-- Phase 2 backfill: batched, no global lock, idempotent
UPDATE orders SET contact_email = email
  WHERE contact_email IS NULL AND id BETWEEN :lo AND :hi;  -- loop :lo/:hi over the table

-- Phase 3 constrain: validate the rule on already-populated data
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT contact_email_present CHECK (contact_email IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT contact_email_present;   -- scans, does not block writes

-- Phase 4 contract: ONLY after the app reads/writes contact_email
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN email;

-- == ROLLBACK (reverse the latest phase only) ==
-- If we are pre-contract, the old column still exists — undo is cheap:
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS contact_email_present;
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS contact_email;        -- back to the prior schema
steps: Expand is the safe move: Adding a NULLABLE column is a metadata change — instant, no row rewrite, no long lock. This is why expand always comes first and is always reversible.

Backfill in batches inside a transaction: Bounding by id keeps each UPDATE small so it never takes a table-wide lock. WHERE contact_email IS NULL makes the migration idempotent — safe to re-run if it dies halfway.

Add the constraint NOT VALID, then VALIDATE: NOT VALID adds the rule instantly for new rows; VALIDATE scans existing rows separately without blocking writes. If a row is null, VALIDATE fails loudly — that is your constraint test, not a surprise outage.

Contract last — and only after cutover: Dropping email is the one irreversible step. It runs only once the app no longer reads the old column, so the expand phases can be rolled back freely until this line.

The rollback IS part of the artifact: Because contract hasn't run, the old column is intact: drop the new constraint and column and you are byte-for-byte back to the prior schema. A migration without this block is not reviewable.

storyboard.say: We start with the old schema: thousands of live rows and a running app already depend on this column named email.
Phase one, expand: add the new contact_email column alongside the old one. Nothing breaks yet, and this step is fully reversible.
Phase two, backfill: copy data into the new column in small batches, so no single statement locks all eighty million rows.
Phase three, constrain: only once every row is filled do we add the NOT NULL, validating the new shape without a long lock.
Phase four, contract: after the app cuts over and stops reading the old column, we finally drop it. Safe because nothing depends on it.
The invariant that makes this safe: every phase is reversible. At any point we can roll back without stranding a single row.
The shortcut skips all of that: one destructive ALTER against the live table at 2 a.m., because the column looked trivial.
And that single ALTER takes a full table lock: every checkout write blocks for eleven minutes and the old data is stranded. That's the failure this packet prevents.

migrations-schema-evolution.text: The senior tell: a migration is reviewed by its rollback, not its forward. Anyone can write an ALTER. The engineer who writes the matching DOWN script — and can name the one phase (contract / drop) that crosses the point of no return — is the one whose migration gets merged. SWEBOK and ABET both frame this as the difference between a change and a controlled, verifiable change.

migrations-schema-evolution.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this migration is not just a happy-path answer.' Which response points to real proof?
options: "It ran green on my local database with no errors."

"Here is the DDL diff, the rollback script that restores the prior schema, the VALIDATE CONSTRAINT run that passed on the existing rows, and the before/after EXPLAIN showing the new query uses the index instead of a seq scan."
"The new column has a sensible name and a comment."
"I added the NOT NULL in one ALTER so there are fewer steps to review."
migrations-schema-evolution.explanation: Only option 2 names inspectable artifacts that span the real risks: the DDL diff (what changed), a rollback (reversibility), a constraint validation against existing data (truth preserved), and a query-plan comparison (the change actually does what it was for). A green local run (1) proves nothing on a populated, concurrently-written table; fewer steps (4) is exactly the destructive shortcut.

A REST API deprecates a field by adding the new one, dual-writing, then removing the old (same three phases). A data pipeline evolves an event schema by tolerating both versions during the cutover. Anywhere existing data and a running consumer both depend on a shape, you expand, migrate, then contract — with a rollback for every phase. query-plans-performance.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) slow query on a table you own, read its actual query plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and write the decision packet: the plan before, the index or rewrite you chose, the rejected option, the plan after, and the rollback. The win is a measured plan change you can defend — not a hunch that an index will help.
query-plans-performance.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md with a before/after EXPLAIN ANALYZE diff (actual rows, actual time, the scan node that changed), the chosen index/rewrite, the rejected option with its reason, a rollback (DROP INDEX) script, and a constraint that stays true under the change. A reviewer reads the two plans and agrees the change is why it got faster.
query-plans-performance.unlock: Your packet shows a real query plan before and after, names the scan that changed (Seq Scan → Index Scan or a join reorder), and includes a rollback — no claim of speedup without the two plans.
query-plans-performance.doNotClaim: Do not claim a query is 'optimized' because you added an index and it 'feels faster'. Wall-clock from a warm cache is not proof — the buffer cache lies. The proof is the plan: the planner now chooses a cheaper node, with lower actual rows scanned, on a cold or representative run. An index the planner refuses to use is dead weight you still pay to maintain on every write.

query-plans-performance.text: The dashboard query that returned in 40ms on your laptop takes 9 seconds in production, and the on-call is staring at a table that grew from 10k rows to 40 million while you slept. Nobody guesses their way out of this — you ask the database one question: show me the plan.

A query plan is the database telling you exactly how it will fetch your data — which index, which scan, which join order, and how many rows it expects at each step. Read it before you touch a schema, because the wrong index is a write-time tax that buys you nothing, and the cheapest fix is often a rewrite, not a new structure.

query-plans-performance.prompt: Your query filters on `email`, there's an index on `email`, and it's still slow. Before you blame the database — why might the planner be ignoring your index? Answer before reading on.
query-plans-performance.reveal: Because for THIS query the index is the slow path, and the planner knows it. If the filter matches 30% of a 40M-row table, jumping to the index and back to the heap 12M times costs more random I/O than just reading the whole table sequentially — so a Seq Scan is correct. Indexes win on selectivity (few rows out of many). Wrap `email` in `LOWER(email)` or a leading-wildcard `LIKE '%x'` and the index becomes unusable entirely. The planner isn't broken; your mental model of 'index = fast' is. EXPLAIN shows you which world you're in.

query-plans-performance.intro: Reading the real plan — before, fix, and after. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
query-plans-performance.code:
-- BEFORE: the slow query, with its actual plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
--  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..921k rows=210000 width=20)
--                       (actual time=0.4..8932 ms  rows=180312  loops=1)
--    Filter: (status = 'open' AND created_at > ...)
--    Rows Removed by Filter: 39819688      <-- read 40M to keep 180k
--  Planning Time: 0.3 ms   Execution Time: 9021 ms

-- THE FIX: a partial composite index matching the WHERE shape
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_open_recent
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'open';   -- partial: only index the rows we query

ANALYZE orders;            -- refresh stats so the planner trusts the index

-- AFTER: same query, re-planned
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
--  Index Scan using idx_orders_open_recent on orders
--                       (actual time=0.05..41 ms  rows=180312  loops=1)
--  Execution Time: 47 ms       <-- 9021 ms -> 47 ms, plan node CHANGED

-- ROLLBACK (two-way door): the index is additive, drop reverses it
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_open_recent;
steps: Measure first, with ANALYZE: EXPLAIN alone shows estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and reports actual rows + actual time. You cannot prove a speedup without the real numbers.
Name the offending node: Seq Scan on orders — the planner reads every row. The 'cost' is the planner's estimate; the 'actual time' is the truth. When they disagree, suspect stale statistics.
The smoking gun: Rows Removed by Filter: 39.8M. The query keeps 180k but the engine touched 40M to find them. That ratio — kept vs scanned — is the selectivity that decides whether an index helps.

A partial composite index: Index created_at, but WHERE status='open' so only open orders are indexed. Smaller index, cheaper writes, and it matches the exact query shape. CONCURRENTLY avoids locking the table in production.

ANALYZE — or the index is invisible: Fresh statistics let the planner trust the new index. Skip this and it may keep choosing the Seq Scan; the index then costs write time and earns nothing — the classic dead-weight failure.
Prove the plan changed: Index Scan using idx_orders_open_recent, 47 ms. The node TYPE changed — that is the proof, not the wall-clock alone. Same actual rows (180312), so the result is identical.
Rollback = the reversal condition: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY reverses cleanly with no data loss. An index migration is a two-way door; this line is what lets you ship it without fear.

query-plans-performance.title: Read the plan before you change the schema
query-plans-performance.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the planner's chosen scan, join order, and estimated-vs-actual rows. The invariant: a measured plan change is the proof of a speedup — never the index alone. If estimate and actual diverge wildly, the planner is flying blind; fix the stats, not the schema.

query-plans-performance.title: How the planner turns SQL into a plan — and where it goes wrong
query-plans-performance.subtitle: The same query takes the slow path (Seq Scan on a giant table) or the fast path (Index Scan). The decision hinges on selectivity and fresh statistics. The dashed edge is the failure: stale stats make the planner mis-estimate rows and pick the wrong scan.

nodes.label: Seq Scan
nodes.description: read all 40M rows — fast only if most rows match

nodes.label: Index Scan
nodes.description: jump via index — fast when few rows match

legend.label: the planner — picks a path by estimated cost
fast path: index used because few rows match
failure path: stale stats → wrong scan

storyboard.say: It starts when a SQL query arrives and hands itself to the query planner, whose job is to parse it and decide how to fetch the data.
The planner doesn't guess blindly — it pulls table statistics to estimate how many rows each step will touch.
When the query is unselective and hits most of the table, the planner picks a sequential scan, reading every row of a giant table.
When selectivity is high and only a few rows match, it chooses an index scan — the fast path that jumps straight to the data.
Either scan produces the same rows, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports the actual rows and time each path really cost.
Here's the failure: stale statistics make the planner mis-estimate rows and choose the wrong scan — 40 milliseconds becomes 9 seconds.
The lesson: when estimated and actual rows diverge wildly, the planner is flying blind — fix the stats, not the schema.

query-plans-performance.caption: Indexing the low-selectivity column (status, 2 distinct values) is the classic trap: the planner refuses it and you pay write cost forever. Selectivity, read from the plan, decides what to index.

query-plans-performance.text: The senior tell: read 'Rows Removed by Filter' and the estimate-vs-actual gap before you read anything else. If the planner expected 200 rows and got 200,000, your statistics are stale — run ANALYZE and re-plan before adding a single index. Half of 'we need an index' incidents are really 'we never ran ANALYZE after a bulk load,' and the planner was mis-estimating selectivity the whole time. Grounded in engineering discipline (and reinforced by SWEBOK V4's emphasis on evidence-based measurement): optimization decisions must be evidence-driven, and the query plan is the evidence. (SWEBOK V4 has no 'data-management knowledge area.')

query-plans-performance.question: A reviewer asks for proof your index actually sped up the query. Which is the convincing evidence?
options: The query ran in 50ms when you re-ran it after creating the index.
An EXPLAIN ANALYZE before (Seq Scan, 9s) and after (Index Scan, 47ms) showing the plan node changed and the same rows were returned.
The index exists — you can see it in \d orders.
Your ORM's query log shows a lower duration on the last request.
query-plans-performance.explanation: Only option 2 is proof. A faster re-run (1, 4) can be warm buffer cache, not the index — the planner might still be doing a Seq Scan over cached pages. The index merely existing (3) says nothing about whether the planner USES it. The before/after plans show the node type changed from Seq Scan to Index Scan with identical rows out — that, and only that, proves the index is the cause.

-- Scenario: an "orders" table. The slow query in the lesson scanned every row
-- filtering on status = 'open' AND a recent created_at range. The fix was a
-- PARTIAL COMPOSITE index that matches exactly that WHERE shape:

--     ON orders (created_at)
--     WHERE status = 'open';
--
-- The index is already created below. Your job: write the query whose filter
-- shape lines up with that index so the planner can use it.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  status      TEXT    NOT NULL,
  total       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at  TEXT    NOT NULL   -- ISO date, sorts lexicographically
);

INSERT INTO orders (id, status, total, created_at) VALUES
  (1,  'open',      120, '2026-06-01'),
  (2,  'shipped',   340, '2026-06-02'),
  (3,  'open',       55, '2026-06-10'),
  (4,  'open',      890, '2026-06-14'),
  (5,  'cancelled', 200, '2026-06-15'),
  (6,  'open',       75, '2026-05-20'),
  (7,  'shipped',   410, '2026-06-16'),
  (8,  'open',      260, '2026-06-16'),
  (9,  'open',      130, '2026-06-17'),
  (10, 'cancelled',  99, '2026-06-12');

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_open_recent
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'open';

If the node is identical, you have not proven the index did anything. · Actual rows returned match before and after — the change made it faster, not different. A speedup that changes results is a bug. · You ran ANALYZE after the index build and confirmed the planner actually chose the index — an index it ignores is dead weight that taxes every write. · A rollback (DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, or the reverse migration) is in the packet, and you marked the change two-way-door — index migrations reverse with no data loss. · The constraint still holds under the change: a UNIQUE or NOT NULL the table guarantees is not weakened by the index or rewrite you chose.

Transfer evidence — apply the database reasoning to a materially different schema or workload: The move travels to every query engine you'll meet. Postgres calls it EXPLAIN ANALYZE; MySQL has EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the FORMAT=TREE output; a data warehouse like BigQuery or Snowflake hands you a query profile with the same skeleton — scan, join order, rows in vs rows out, the spilled stage that's actually slow. What stays invariant: read the plan before you change the structure, prove the change by the node that moved, and never trust wall-clock over the plan. What changes is the cost model — a warehouse punishes a full-table shuffle, an OLTP store punishes random heap fetches — so the same plan can be right in one and wrong in the other. Your schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md is the first artifact of the database capstone: it already carries a before/after plan, a chosen-vs-rejected option, a constraint that survives the change, and a rollback. The capstone reuses it unchanged in structure — you don't talk about query performance now, you can prove it.

repository-data-access-layer.text: A 5-minute column rename — orders.total → total_cents — fans out into 47 broken call sites across three services, because every one of them wrote its own SELECT against the table.
