In the production-pressure phase, schemas change under load: columns rename, indexes get added, tables split. The repository is the seam that absorbs that change — it concentrates every query, constraint assumption, and transaction boundary for one entity in one swappable place, so migrations stay local.

repository-data-access-layer.prompt: Your service has SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 written in 12 different files. A migration renames a column. How many files break — and what does that tell you about where the schema actually lives? Answer before reading on.

seed-fixtures-test-data.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'test data' if your seed uses NOW(), random IDs, or relies on insertion order for keys. That is non-deterministic data wearing a fixture's clothes — the test that depends on it is flaky by construction, and a flaky fixture is worse than none.

seed-fixtures-test-data.text: The suite is green on your laptop and red in CI — same code, same tests. The difference is the data: your local DB still holds yesterday's rows, and a fixture quietly assumed user id 7 already existed. A test that depends on leftover state is not a test; it is a coin flip.

Sitting in the production-pressure phase of Databases and Data Modeling, seed fixtures are the known, controlled data state every other database skill is verified against — migrations, query plans, constraint tests, and the capstone all stand on fixtures that say the same thing every run.

seed-fixtures-test-data.prompt: Your test inserts an order, then asserts the dashboard shows '1 order today'. It passes 100 times, then fails at midnight UTC. Why — before reading on?
seed-fixtures-test-data.reveal: The fixture used NOW() for the order timestamp, and 'today' rolled over mid-run. The data was never fixed — it drifted with the wall clock. A real fixture pins time: insert the order at a frozen reference instant ('2024-01-01 12:00:00Z') so 'today' is whatever YOU defined, not whatever the clock happened to read. Non-determinism in seed data is the #1 source of tests that pass until they don't.

seed-fixtures-test-data.intro: A deterministic seed, one line at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: Wrap in a transaction: BEGIN/COMMIT makes the whole seed atomic: if any constraint fails, the DB rolls back to empty rather than half-loaded. Isolation means a parallel test never sees a partial fixture.
Reset first → idempotency: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE clears the tables and resets sequences so re-running yields the IDENTICAL state. This is what makes the seed safe to run twice.
Fixed IDs + frozen clock: Explicit ids (1,2) and a literal timestamp — never auto-increment-by-order or NOW(). The test can assert 'user 1' and '12:00:00' because YOU pinned them.
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: Belt-and-suspenders idempotency: even without the TRUNCATE, a second load won't raise a duplicate-key error. The UNIQUE constraint stays satisfied.
Parents before children: Orders carry a FK to users. Seed users first or every INSERT violates the foreign-key constraint. Insertion ORDER is part of the contract.
Fast-forward the sequence: After hand-setting IDs, bump the sequence past them so app-generated INSERTs don't collide with fixture IDs — a classic post-seed footgun.

storyboard.say: Every test run starts from an empty schema, then the seed loads the controlled data the whole suite depends on.
After seeding, the database has to commit — but only if every constraint holds: unique keys, foreign keys, all of it.
The failure path: NOW() drifts, a duplicate key collides, or a child row references a parent that was never seeded — the seed fails.
You repair the seed by pinning the clock, using ON CONFLICT for idempotency, and inserting parents before children.
With constraints satisfied, the seed commits into a known, controlled state — the same rows every single run.
Only now does the test read from that known state and assert — because the data underneath it is guaranteed, not accidental.
After each test, teardown runs and resets the schema back to empty — re-loadable, so the next run starts identical.
That loop is the invariant: load twice, get the same state; tear down, get empty — or the downstream test is a coin flip.

'I ran the seed on an empty schema, then ran it again — identical row counts, no error; I removed the user INSERT and the order INSERT failed the FK check; teardown returned the DB to zero rows.'
'The fixtures cover every column in the table.'
'I used realistic-looking names and emails for the rows.'

seed-fixtures-test-data.starter:
-- Schema: orders.user_id references users.id (FK).
CREATE TABLE users (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  placed_at   TEXT NOT NULL
);

-- TODO: Write the seed fixtures below.
-- Rules from the lesson:
--   1. Insert PARENT rows (users) before CHILD rows (orders) so every
--      order.user_id points at a user that already exists (FK-safe).
--   2. Use FIXED timestamp literals, never NOW()/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, so the
--      data is identical on every run (deterministic).
-- Seed exactly these fixtures:
--   users:  id 1 ada@example.test, id 2 lin@example.test, id 3 mei@example.test
--           (all created_at '2024-01-01T12:00:00Z')
--   orders: id 10 -> user 1, 4200 cents
--           id 11 -> user 1,  800 cents
--           id 12 -> user 2,  900 cents
--           (all placed_at '2024-01-01T12:00:00Z')
-- NOTE: user 3 (mei) intentionally has NO orders.

-- INSERT INTO users ... ;
-- INSERT INTO orders ... ;

-- Report (do not edit): per-user order count and total.
SELECT u.email AS email,
       COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total_cents), 0) AS total_cents
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.email

seed-fixtures-test-data.symptom: Tests pass when run alone but fail when the suite runs in parallel: 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint users_email_key'. The fixture itself looks correct.
seed-fixtures-test-data.task: Two tests share this seed and both run it. Find why parallel runs collide, and fix it so the fixture is idempotent and isolated. Keep the repaired failure case as a regression check so the defect cannot silently return.
seed-fixtures-test-data.fix: The seed has no reset and no conflict handling, so the second test re-inserts id 1 and hits the UNIQUE constraint. Add `TRUNCATE orders, users RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;` at the top (or `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING` on each INSERT) and a teardown after each test. Better: give each parallel worker its own transaction that ROLLBACKs at test end (isolation), so workers never share committed fixture rows at all.

seed-fixtures-test-data.intro: Prove your fixtures hold — no vibes:
items: Run the seed on an empty schema, then run it again. If row counts differ or it errors on the second run, it is not idempotent — add TRUNCATE/RESTART IDENTITY or ON CONFLICT.
Grep the seed for NOW(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, and random IDs. Any dynamic value is non-determinism — replace it with a fixed literal.
Delete one parent row's INSERT and re-run: a child INSERT must fail the foreign-key constraint. If it doesn't, your FK is missing or deferred — the fixture isn't testing what you think.
Run the teardown and SELECT count(*) on every fixture table. Anything but zero means rows leak into the next test.
Run the suite twice in a row WITHOUT manually resetting the DB. If the second run fails, a test depends on leftover state, not on the fixture.

data-quality-checks.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) table and write a Data Quality Checks suite: at least four falsifiable assertions over a known invariant — not-null on a required column, a uniqueness/key check, a referential check across a relationship, and a domain/range constraint — each phrased so a bad row makes it FAIL loudly, not pass quietly.
data-quality-checks.proof: The artifact data_quality_contract.sql attached to the evidence ledger: 4+ named checks, each with the invariant it guards, the exact failing row it would catch, and a run transcript showing it returns rows (FAIL) on dirty data and zero rows (PASS) on clean data. A reviewer can run it without you narrating.
data-quality-checks.unlock: Each check names an invariant, is falsifiable (a wrong row makes it fail), and you have a transcript proving it both passes on clean data and fails on a seeded bad row.
data-quality-checks.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'have data quality checks' if every check returns zero rows because it can only ever pass. A check that cannot fail is decoration, not a check. Each assertion must be able to surface a violating row — and you must have seen it do so at least once.

data-quality-checks.text: The migration shipped green, the dashboard turned up, and three weeks later finance finds duplicate order_ids inflating revenue 4% — the constraint that would have caught it on row one was never written. Bad data does not announce itself; it compounds in silence until someone trusts a number that was never true.

This lesson opens Module 4 in the production-pressure phase: a schema change must preserve integrity while supporting a new query path and a rollback plan. A data quality check is the enforceable, falsifiable assertion that turns 'the data is probably fine' into Section 1 of the migration packet you carry through this module.

data-quality-checks.prompt: Your orders table has a NOT NULL constraint on customer_id and a foreign key to customers. Is your data quality already guaranteed? Answer before reading on.
data-quality-checks.reveal: No — constraints only enforce what they were declared on, going forward. They say nothing about rows that predate them, nothing about a customer_id that points to a soft-deleted customer, nothing about an amount of -$40, and nothing about the 6% of rows where status is 'shipped' but shipped_at is NULL. The schema enforces shape; data quality checks enforce truth. The gap between them is exactly where silent corruption lives.

data-quality-checks.intro: Writing the quality contract, one check at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
data-quality-checks.code:
-- data_quality_contract.sql  · invariant set for orders (run pre-promote AND post-migration)

-- CHECK 1 (completeness): every order must name a customer
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL;

-- CHECK 2 (uniqueness): order_id is a key — no duplicates may exist
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- CHECK 3 (referential): no order may point to a missing/soft-deleted customer
SELECT o.id FROM orders o
  LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.id IS NULL OR c.deleted_at IS NOT NULL;

-- CHECK 4 (domain): amount must be >= 0, and 'shipped' implies a shipped_at
SELECT id FROM orders
  WHERE amount < 0
     OR (status = 'shipped' AND shipped_at IS NULL);

-- PASS contract: all four queries return ZERO rows. Any returned row is a violation.
steps: The contract header: One file, run at the same two moments every migration: before promoting staged rows, and again right after the schema change — the rollback plan keys off these results.
Completeness check: The query returns rows that VIOLATE the not-null invariant. Phrasing it as 'find the bad rows' is what makes it falsifiable — empty result = pass.

Uniqueness check: GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 surfaces duplicate order_ids a UNIQUE constraint would have blocked on insert — but catches the ones already in the table from before the constraint existed.
Referential check: An FK alone won't catch a customer that was SOFT-deleted after the order was written. The LEFT JOIN finds orphans the constraint silently allows.
Domain / range check: Two invariants in one: amount can't be negative, and a 'shipped' status must have a timestamp. This is the state-consistency rule a column type can't express.
The pass rule: Empty across all four = PASS. This is the line that makes the file a contract: a reviewer runs it and reads the result, no narration needed.

data-quality-checks.title: A quality check is a falsifiable assertion over an invariant — it must be able to FAIL
data-quality-checks.text: Name the invariant (the thing that must always be true), write a query whose result is the set of rows that VIOLATE it, and assert that set is empty. The invariant: a check earns its place only if a bad row makes it fail loudly. A check that can only pass proves nothing.

data-quality-checks.title: Where checks sit on the write → store → trust path
data-quality-checks.subtitle: Six stages from ingest to a trusted query. Checks gate the load and run again post-migration; the failure path (silent bad rows reaching the dashboard) is what the quality contract exists to cut off.

nodes.label: Silent Corruption
nodes.description: dup keys · orphan FKs · bad domain

legend.label: the quality gate (the whole skill)
failure path — silent corruption
promote only on PASS

storyboard.say: Every record starts here: an external source drops raw orders into a staging load before anything touches the trusted table.
Between staging and the table sits the quality gate — the one place where we assert the invariants that must always hold.
The invariant here: order_ids must be unique. We write a query that returns the rows that violate it, and assert that set is empty.
If nothing violates the rule, the gate passes and promotes the batch into the trusted Orders Table.
If duplicates show up, the gate fails loudly and quarantines the batch — bad rows never reach production.
Only promoted rows feed the dashboard, so the numbers finance trusts rest on an invariant that was actually enforced.
Skip the gate and corruption leaks straight through — silent duplicates inflating revenue until someone trusts a number that was never checked.

data-quality-checks.text: Standards grounding (SWEBOK V4 Software Quality, which defines a general data quality model): the senior tell is treating a quality rule as an executable, falsifiable assertion versioned alongside the schema — not a paragraph in a runbook. (SWEBOK defines data-quality characteristics but does not prescribe executable assertions versioned with a schema; that specific practice is the author's, not the standard's.) If your check isn't a query you can run in CI and watch turn red, it isn't enforced; it's a hope. data-quality-checks.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your data quality checks aren't just happy-path answers. What do you point to?
options: The PR comment saying all checks returned zero rows.
A transcript showing each check returning the seeded violating row (FAIL) on dirty data and zero rows (PASS) after the fix — proving each assertion can fail.
The list of NOT NULL and FOREIGN KEY constraints already in the schema.
A note that the data 'looked correct' after the migration.
data-quality-checks.explanation: A check that has only ever returned zero rows might be enforcing nothing — you can't tell a real pass from a check that can't fail. The evidence is the demonstrated FAIL-then-PASS transcript: it proves the assertion is falsifiable AND that the violation it guards against is now absent. The schema constraints (3) cover shape going forward but not pre-existing or state-consistency invariants; 'looked correct' (4) is exactly the vibe this lesson kills.

data-quality-checks.starter:
-- Data-quality contract lab · SQLite (sql.js), runs fresh in your browser.
-- In the lesson, a PASSING check returns ZERO rows; any returned row is a violation to fix.
-- Here we INVERT that: your job is to LIST the violating orders so a human can triage them.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER,
  amount      REAL,
  status      TEXT,
  shipped_at  TEXT      -- ISO date, or NULL if not yet shipped
);

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount, status, shipped_at) VALUES
  (1, 100,  49.99, 'shipped',    '2026-06-01'),  -- clean
  (2, 101,  -5.00, 'refunded',    NULL),          -- BAD: amount < 0
  (3, 102, 120.00, 'shipped',     NULL),          -- BAD: shipped but no shipped_at
  (4, 103,   0.00, 'pending',     NULL),          -- clean (0 is allowed)
  (5, 104, -19.50, 'shipped',     NULL),          -- BAD: amount < 0 AND shipped w/o date
  (6, 105,  75.25, 'shipped',    '2026-06-10'),   -- clean
  (7, 106,  10.00, 'pending',     NULL);          -- clean

-- DOMAIN INVARIANT: amount must be >= 0, and status='shipped' implies shipped_at IS NOT NULL.
-- TODO: SELECT the id of every order that VIOLATES the invariant.
-- Return one column named "id", ordered by id ascending.

data-quality-checks.symptom: The uniqueness check reports PASS on a table you KNOW has duplicate order_ids — finance found them last week.
data-quality-checks.brokenCode:
-- 'uniqueness' check
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_id IS NOT NULL;
data-quality-checks.task: This query can only ever pass (it returns every non-null order_id, which the author reads as 'they all exist'). Rewrite it so it returns ONLY the rows that violate the uniqueness invariant — and explain why the original is theater. Keep the repaired failure case as a regression check so the defect cannot silently return.
data-quality-checks.fix: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;  — The original checked presence, not uniqueness: 'is the column populated' instead of 'is the key actually unique'. A check must return the VIOLATING set (duplicates), so an empty result is the only thing that means PASS. The duplicate-key incident was invisible because the check could not express the invariant it claimed to guard.

backup-restore-retention.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) production database and write a Backup, Restore & Retention policy that proves recovery — not just that backups exist. Define the recovery objectives (RPO/RTO), a tested restore drill, and a retention schedule with a documented expiry, then attach it to the evidence ledger.
backup-restore-retention.proof: The `schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md` artifact gains a Backup/Restore/Retention section: stated RPO + RTO, a restore-drill transcript (backup → restore to a scratch instance → row-count + checksum match), and a retention schedule with a defended expiry. A reviewer can point to the restore transcript, not just the backup job's green checkmark.
backup-restore-retention.unlock: Your policy names an RPO and RTO, includes a transcript of an actually-executed restore that verified the data, and a retention schedule whose expiry you can defend.
backup-restore-retention.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have backups if you have never restored one. A backup that has never been restored is an untested hypothesis, not a recovery plan. The invariant of this skill is the restore, not the dump — 'the cron ran green' is theatre until a restore reproduces the data.

backup-restore-retention.text: The migration dropped a column at 2 a.m. and the rollback script had a typo, so the team reaches for last night's backup — and discovers the nightly dump has been silently writing a zero-byte file for three weeks. The backups existed. None of them restored.

Schema design, constraints, and migrations all assume the data underneath survives a bad change. Backup, Restore & Retention is the safety net that makes a destructive migration reversible — Section 5 of the same `schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md` you carry through this course, the part a reviewer trusts only when a restore has actually run.

backup-restore-retention.prompt: "We run a nightly pg_dump to S3 and the job is green." Before you call that a backup strategy — what is the unproven assumption hiding in it? Answer before reading on.
backup-restore-retention.reveal: Two assumptions, both untested: that the dump contains restorable data, and that you can restore it inside your recovery-time target. A green job proves a file was written, not that the file restores. The real invariant is RPO/RTO met by a *tested* restore: how much data you can lose (RPO) and how fast you can be back (RTO). Most 'backup outages' are restore failures — corrupt dumps, missing roles, an unrecoverable WAL gap — discovered for the first time during the incident.

backup-restore-retention.intro: The restore drill — the proof, line by line. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
backup-restore-retention.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP="s3://db-backups/orders/$(date -d yesterday +%F).dump"
SCRATCH="orders_restore_check"
RPO_MAX_MIN=15   # we accept losing at most 15 min of writes
RTO_MAX_MIN=30   # we must be queryable again within 30 min

start=$(date +%s)
aws s3 cp "$BACKUP" /tmp/restore.dump
[ -s /tmp/restore.dump ] || { echo "FAIL: backup is zero-byte"; exit 1; }

dropdb --if-exists "$SCRATCH" && createdb "$SCRATCH"
pg_restore --no-owner --exit-on-error -d "$SCRATCH" /tmp/restore.dump

rows=$(psql -tAc "SELECT count(*) FROM orders" "$SCRATCH")
sum=$(psql -tAc "SELECT md5(string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id)) FROM orders" "$SCRATCH")
elapsed_min=$(( ($(date +%s) - start) / 60 ))

echo "restored rows=$rows checksum=$sum in ${elapsed_min}m"
[ "$elapsed_min" -le "$RTO_MAX_MIN" ] || { echo "FAIL: RTO ${elapsed_min}m > ${RTO_MAX_MIN}m"; exit 1; }
[ "$rows" -gt 0 ] || { echo "FAIL: restored table is empty"; exit 1; }
echo "PASS: RPO<=${RPO_MAX_MIN}m, RTO=${elapsed_min}m, data verified"
steps: Point at a REAL backup: Yesterday's actual dump, not a fixture. If the drill never touches production artifacts, it proves nothing about production recovery.

Declare RPO and RTO as numbers: RPO = max acceptable data loss (15 min). RTO = max acceptable downtime (30 min). These are the contract the restore must satisfy — a backup with no objectives can't pass or fail.
Catch the zero-byte failure first: `-s` fails on an empty file — the exact silent failure from the mission. The cheapest disqualifier runs before the expensive restore.
Restore to SCRATCH, never the primary: `--exit-on-error` makes a partial restore a failure, not a warning. You restore to a throwaway DB so the drill is safe to run on a schedule.

Verify the DATA, not just exit code 0: Row count plus a content checksum. A restore can exit 0 and still hand you an empty or truncated table — the checksum is what turns 'it ran' into 'the data is there'.

Assert against RTO, then PASS: If the restore blew the 30-minute budget, it FAILS even with correct data — slow recovery is a failed recovery during an outage. The PASS line is the transcript you attach to the packet.

storyboard.say: The live primary is the source of truth. Everything on this map exists so a destructive migration against it stays reversible.
Two streams leave the primary: a nightly base backup dumps the whole database, and the WAL archive ships every change continuously.
Both streams write into the backup store. Base plus WAL is what gives you point-in-time recovery, not just last night.
Here is the decision that saves you: a restore drill pulls from the store and rebuilds it to scratch, never onto the live primary.
The drill is what catches a corrupt or zero-byte dump before the incident, instead of at 2 a.m. with the rollback already failed.
A retention sweep expires old backups but keeps your defended window, so the store stays bounded and the RPO stays honest.
The invariant: the restore is the deliverable, never the dump. A backup you have never restored is a file, not a safety net.

backup-restore-retention.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this isn't just a happy-path answer." Which proves your backup policy is real?
options: A screenshot of the nightly backup cron job showing a green checkmark for the last 30 days.
A transcript of a restore drill: a real backup restored to a scratch DB, row count and checksum matching, completed inside the stated RTO.
A list of every backup file in the S3 bucket with their sizes and timestamps.
A note in the runbook saying 'backups are configured and monitored.'
backup-restore-retention.explanation: Only option 2 proves recovery. The green cron (1) and the file list (3) prove dumps were *written* — the exact thing that was true in the mission while every dump was zero bytes. A runbook note (4) is an assertion, not evidence. The restore transcript is the only artifact that demonstrates the data comes back, intact, within RTO — the invariant of this skill.

backup-restore-retention.title: Verify a restored backup: prove parity and check the recovery window
backup-restore-retention.summary: Write one SQL query (run it in the browser) that joins each nightly restore-drill against the source orders count, computes row deltas and elapsed restore minutes, and flags whether each drill met the RTO target and had zero-drift parity — the automated integrity check a restore runbook performs.
backup-restore-retention.starter:
-- Scenario: nightly disaster-recovery drills.
-- Every night a backup of the production `orders` table is restored into a
-- scratch DB and verified. A drill PASSES only if:
--   (1) restored_rows == source_rows for that day  (zero-drift parity), AND
--   (2) elapsed restore time <= the RTO target (30 minutes).
--
-- source_rows = the true production row count captured at backup time.
-- restored_rows / elapsed_min = what the restore drill actually measured.

CREATE TABLE restore_drills (
  drill_date     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,  -- YYYY-MM-DD
  source_rows    INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- prod count at backup time
  restored_rows  INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- rows found after pg_restore
  elapsed_min    INTEGER NOT NULL   -- restore + verify wall-clock minutes
);

INSERT INTO restore_drills (drill_date, source_rows, restored_rows, elapsed_min) VALUES
  ('2026-06-13', 480200, 480200, 22),  -- clean
  ('2026-06-14', 481050, 481050, 41),  -- clean rows but too slow (RTO breach)
  ('2026-06-15', 482310, 482297, 19),  -- fast but 13 rows short (drift)
  ('2026-06-16', 483500, 483500, 30),  -- clean, exactly at the RTO limit
  ('2026-06-17', 484900, 484915, 28);  -- extra 15 rows (drift, wrong direction)

-- RTO target is 30 minutes. Parity means restored_rows = source_rows.
-- TODO: return one row per drill (ordered by drill_date) with columns:
--   drill_date,
--   row_delta  = restored_rows - source_rows,
--   elapsed_min,
--   verdict    = 'PASS' when parity AND elapsed_min <= 30, else 'FAIL'

security-privacy-compliance.outcome: Take one table that holds PII (users, with email, name, ssn_last4, marketing_consent) and write the Security & Privacy section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the threat you defend, the access constraint enforced IN the database (row-level security + least-privilege role), the encryption boundary for the sensitive column, and the GDPR-correct deletion path — with a rollback that cannot leak.
security-privacy-compliance.proof: The Security & Privacy section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: a named threat, an RLS policy that the app role cannot bypass, one column moved behind an encryption boundary, a deletion path that satisfies erasure WITHOUT breaking referential integrity, and a rollback script proven not to re-expose deleted PII. A reviewer with the app credentials runs SELECT and cannot read another tenant's rows.
security-privacy-compliance.unlock: Your packet enforces access in the database (not just the app), names the encryption boundary, and proves the deletion + rollback path cannot re-expose PII.
security-privacy-compliance.doNotClaim: Do not claim the data is 'secured' because the application checks permissions. App-layer checks are bypassed the moment anyone connects with the same DB credentials — a script, a BI tool, a leaked connection string. If the constraint is not enforced by the database, you have a convention, not a control.

security-privacy-compliance.text: A regulator's letter arrives: a user invoked their right to erasure 40 days ago and just found their data still queryable in your analytics replica. The DELETE ran — but a foreign key from orders silently soft-failed, the row survived in a backup snapshot, and a nightly job restored it. One missing constraint became a reportable breach.

Security, privacy, and compliance are not a layer you bolt on after the schema works — they are invariants the schema must hold under change, load, and bad input. This lesson turns 'we should protect PII' into a reviewable migration packet that enforces access, encryption, and erasure inside the database itself.

security-privacy-compliance.prompt: Your app code carefully checks `if (user.tenant_id === row.tenant_id)` before returning every row. Is the tenant's data isolated? Answer before reading on.
security-privacy-compliance.reveal: No — it is isolated only as long as every query in the company forever routes through that one code path. The analytics job, the data-science notebook, the on-call engineer's psql session, and the next teammate's new endpoint all connect with the same database role and see every tenant's rows. Isolation that lives in application code is a promise; isolation that lives in a row-level-security policy on the table is a control. The database, not the app, has to refuse the read.

security-privacy-compliance.intro: The migration that enforces the controls. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: Encryption boundary: ssn_last4 moves into a bytea encrypted with a key the DB never stores in plaintext. The migration is a transaction — if encryption fails mid-table, the whole step rolls back and no half-encrypted state ships.

The isolation constraint: The policy IS the control: a row is invisible unless its tenant_id matches the session's tenant. This holds for psql, BI tools, and next quarter's new endpoint — none of them can opt out.
Least privilege: app_rw gets DML, never DDL. A compromised app credential cannot DROP the policy or ALTER the table to disable RLS.

Partial index on live rows: Indexing WHERE deleted_at IS NULL keeps the hot path fast AND keeps tombstoned (erased) rows out of the index that feeds normal queries — privacy and performance from one constraint.

Erasure without orphans: Erase by nulling PII + tombstoning, NOT hard DELETE — orders.user_id keeps a valid FK target, so referential integrity survives while the personal data is gone. SECURITY DEFINER runs it under a controlled role.

storyboard.say: A single client sends two very different requests to the same door: read my data, and erase my data. Both land on the App Service.
The app does an access check in code, then queries the database. But it never touches the table directly — it acts through the app_rw role.
The real, enforced control lives here: an RLS policy under a least-privilege role filters rows at the store, no matter what the app intended.
Prove it: even if the app tries to bypass its own check and hit the table, the database still blocks the rows it isn't allowed to see.
Now erasure gets hard. The users table isn't alone — every row streams out to an analytics replica the DELETE must also reach.
And every row is captured in backup snapshots. A deleted user can survive here and get restored by a nightly job forty days later.
The lesson: privacy is an invariant the schema holds under bypass and replication — enforced at the store, and erasure must cover replica and backup too.

security-privacy-compliance.text: Standards grounding: GDPR Art. 17 (erasure) and Art. 32 (security of processing) both demand the control be effective, not merely intended — which is why reviewers look for FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, not ENABLE. ENABLE leaves the table owner exempt, so a single migration connection or admin tool quietly defeats your tenant isolation. The senior tell on a privacy migration is that the author can name who is still exempt from the policy — and has closed that gap on purpose. (SWEBOK V4 Software Security; ABET Computing Outcomes.)

-- Security, privacy & compliance in the database itself.
--
-- In Postgres the lesson enforced two rules structurally:
--   * TENANT ISOLATION  -> a row-level-security policy:  tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')
--   * ERASURE / SOFT DELETE -> a partial index over live rows only:  WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
--
-- SQLite has no RLS, so here you write the query a correctly-scoped
-- app role would run: restrict to one tenant AND exclude erased rows.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id    TEXT    NOT NULL,
  email        TEXT    NOT NULL,
  ssn_last4    TEXT,          -- would be encrypted at the boundary in prod
  deleted_at   TEXT           -- NULL = live; a timestamp = erased (soft-deleted)
);

INSERT INTO users (id, tenant_id, email, ssn_last4, deleted_at) VALUES
  (1, 'acme',   'ada@acme.io',    '1234', NULL),
  (2, 'acme',   'grace@acme.io',  '5678', NULL),
  (3, 'acme',   'alan@acme.io',   '9012', '2026-01-15'),  -- erased under right-to-erasure
  (4, 'globex', 'root@globex.io', '3456', NULL),          -- different tenant: must not leak
  (5, 'globex', 'eve@globex.io',  '7890', NULL),          -- different tenant: must not leak
  (6, 'acme',   'linus@acme.io',  '2222', NULL);

-- Order by id so the result is deterministic.

caching-read-models.outcome: Take one read-heavy query that is straining your source-of-truth tables and design a cached read model for it — then write the decision-and-rollback packet that names the staleness contract, the invalidation trigger, and the consistency you are trading away.

A reviewer agrees the cache can go stale safely and recover without serving wrong totals as if they were authoritative.

caching-read-models.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'cached the read model' if you cannot say how stale a served row may be or what invalidates it. A cache with no staleness bound and no invalidation trigger is not a read model — it is silent data corruption with good latency.

caching-read-models.text: The dashboard 'Total Revenue' tile loads in 40 ms and everyone loves it — until finance notices it has read $2.1M for six hours while three refunds and a chargeback landed in Postgres. The number was fast, authoritative-looking, and wrong, because nobody wrote down when the cache was allowed to lie.

A read model is a precomputed, query-shaped copy of data that exists so a hot read path never re-derives the same aggregate against your normalized tables under load. It sits in the synthesis phase of this course because it only works once you can reason about the source schema, its constraints, and the transaction that keeps the cache and the truth from drifting apart.

caching-read-models.prompt: Your orders dashboard is slow, so you add a `dashboard_totals` table that stores the precomputed revenue per day. What is the one question that decides whether this is a read model or a future incident? Answer before reading on.
caching-read-models.reveal: Not 'is it faster' — it is 'when this row disagrees with the orders table, who wins and how does it heal?' A read model is a denormalized copy, so it WILL drift from the source of truth the moment a write lands and the copy lags. The skill is not building the cache; it is naming the staleness window the business accepts and the invalidation trigger that closes it. Without those two, you have not cached a read model — you have forked the truth and lost the fork.

caching-read-models.intro: The read model + its invalidation, end to end. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
caching-read-models.code:
-- 1. The read model: a query-shaped, derived copy (NOT the source of truth)
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS
SELECT order_date,
       SUM(amount_cents) AS revenue_cents,
       COUNT(*)         AS order_count,
       now()            AS derived_at
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'settled'
GROUP BY order_date;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON daily_revenue (order_date);  -- enables CONCURRENT refresh

-- 2. Staleness contract: a served row may lag the orders table by <= 60s.
--    The dashboard reads daily_revenue, never SUM(orders) live.

-- 3. Invalidation trigger: every settled write enqueues a refresh.
CREATE FUNCTION enqueue_revenue_refresh() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO refresh_queue(model, order_date) VALUES ('daily_revenue', NEW.order_date)
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;          -- coalesce a burst into one rebuild
  RETURN NEW;
END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_settled_refresh
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF status, amount_cents ON orders
  FOR EACH ROW WHEN (NEW.status = 'settled')
  EXECUTE FUNCTION enqueue_revenue_refresh();

-- 4. Rebuild (worker, off the read path): heals the copy back to the source.
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_revenue;  -- no read lock
steps: The derived copy: daily_revenue is a precomputed aggregate of orders. It is a COPY — orders stays the source of truth. derived_at stamps how fresh each row is, so staleness is measurable, not a vibe.

Unique index = concurrent refresh: Without a unique index, REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY is illegal and you must take a read lock. This one line is the difference between a rebuild that blocks the dashboard and one that doesn't.
The staleness contract: Write the bound down: a served row may lag by <= 60s. This is the consistency you are trading for latency — name it so finance can sign it, not discover it.

Invalidation on commit: Every settled write enqueues a refresh keyed by order_date. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING coalesces a burst of refunds into one rebuild — the invalidation trigger the cache lives or dies by.
Scoped, conditional trigger: Fires only on status='settled' writes — not on every column update. A trigger that fires on everything turns your write path into a refresh storm.
Rebuild heals back to truth: CONCURRENTLY rebuilds off the read path with no read lock. This is the repair path on the diagram: the copy reconciles to Postgres, closing the staleness window.

storyboard.say: Start at the entry point: the dashboard reads the 'Total Revenue' tile straight from the read model, never the raw tables.
The read model is a precomputed, query-shaped copy — that's why it loads in 40 ms instead of aggregating orders live.
Meanwhile the Orders Service writes to Postgres, which stays the single source of truth for every refund and chargeback.
On commit the writer emits an invalidation event that re-derives the read model — this is the repair path that heals the cache.
Here's the failure: read the model before the rebuild lands and you serve a stale number as if it were authoritative.
That's the $2.1M bug — six hours stale because nobody wrote down how long the cache was allowed to lie.
The invariant closes the loop: the read model must always reconcile back to Postgres — lag is fine, contradiction is not.
So write down two things: how stale a served row may be, and what re-derives it — an event or a TTL.

  EXECUTE FUNCTION enqueue_revenue_refresh();

-- 4. Rebuild (worker, off the read path): heals the copy back to the source.
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_revenue;  -- no read lock

steps.label: The derived copy
steps.note: daily_revenue is a precomputed aggregate of orders. It is a COPY — orders stays the source of truth. derived_at stamps how fresh each row is, so staleness is measurable, not a vibe.

steps.label: Unique index = concurrent refresh
steps.note: Without a unique index, REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY is illegal and you must take a read lock. This one line is the difference between a rebuild that blocks the dashboard and one that doesn't.

steps.label: The staleness contract
steps.note: Write the bound down: a served row may lag by <= 60s. This is the consistency you are trading for latency — name it so finance can sign it, not discover it.

steps.label: Invalidation on commit
steps.note: Every settled write enqueues a refresh keyed by order_date. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING coalesces a burst of refunds into one rebuild — the invalidation trigger the cache lives or dies by.

steps.label: Scoped, conditional trigger
steps.note: Fires only on status='settled' writes — not on every column update. A trigger that fires on everything turns your write path into a refresh storm.

steps.label: Rebuild heals back to truth
steps.note: CONCURRENTLY rebuilds off the read path with no read lock. This is the repair path on the diagram: the copy reconciles to Postgres, closing the staleness window.

caching-read-models.text: The senior tell: they design the cache MISS, not the cache hit. Anyone can serve the precomputed row. The judgment is in what happens when the read model is missing, mid-rebuild, or past its staleness bound — do you serve stale-but-flagged, fall back to the source query, or fail closed? SWEBOK V4's data-quality (Software Quality) and operability (Software Engineering Operations) axes support this: a read model without a defined behavior on staleness and on rebuild failure has no recovery story, and a cache with no recovery story is a future incident wearing a latency win. (SWEBOK does not discuss caches or read models specifically; the mapping is inference.)

caching-read-models.question: You add a materialized read model for a dashboard total. Which fact most determines whether it is production-safe rather than a silent-corruption risk?
options: It returns in under 50ms on the read path.
It defines a bounded staleness window AND an invalidation trigger that re-derives it from the source of truth, so it can lag but always reconciles.
It is stored in a faster engine than Postgres.
It precomputes every aggregate the dashboard might ever need.
caching-read-models.explanation: A read model is a derived copy, so drift from the source is guaranteed, not hypothetical. Safety comes from a named staleness bound plus an invalidation/rebuild trigger that reconciles the copy back to truth — that is what makes 'stale' mean 'bounded and self-healing' instead of 'silently wrong'. Latency (1), engine choice (3), and coverage (4) are real but secondary; none of them stop the cache from contradicting the source forever.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.outcome: Take one operational table that an analytics team wants to query, and write the Boundary section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: where the OLTP source of truth ends, where the warehouse begins, what crosses the boundary (and what must NOT), and the rollback if the new query path corrupts integrity.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.proof: The Boundary + Decision + Rollback sections of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the source-of-truth table named, the directed sync edge (OLTP -> warehouse) marked as one-way, the constraint that is NOT allowed to be enforced in the warehouse, the PII column held back, and a rollback script that drops the new read path without touching the operational schema. A reviewer can trace one row from write to dashboard and name exactly where truth lives.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.unlock: Your packet names the source of truth, marks the sync as one-directional, lists what does NOT cross the boundary, and the rollback leaves the OLTP schema byte-for-byte unchanged.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'set a warehouse boundary' if analytics queries hit the live OLTP tables directly, or if the warehouse can write back into the operational store. A shared table queried by both sides is not a boundary; it is a collision waiting for a long-running analytical scan to lock your checkout path.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.text: A data analyst runs one innocent SELECT ... GROUP BY over the live orders table to build a quarterly chart; the unindexed full scan takes a row-level lock path, checkout latency spikes to 9 seconds, and the on-call gets paged for an outage that was really a missing boundary.

This is the synthesis lesson where schema, constraints, indexes, transactions, query plans, and privacy all collide at one seam: the line between the operational store that must stay correct under load and the analytics warehouse that must stay flexible for questions. Get the boundary wrong and analytics either corrupts truth or takes the transactional system down with it.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.prompt: Your warehouse is a copy of production tables. To keep reports accurate, should you also copy the OLTP foreign-key and unique constraints into the warehouse? Decide before reading on.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.reveal: No -- and that 'oh' is the boundary. A warehouse is a derived, denormalized, append-friendly read model; enforcing OLTP constraints there fights its job. A late-arriving fact or a soft-deleted dimension row will violate a foreign key and reject good analytical data. The warehouse trusts the source of truth UPSTREAM; it does not re-litigate integrity downstream. Constraints live where writes are authoritative -- the OLTP side -- not where you only read.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.intro: Writing the Boundary + Rollback section, one line at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: Name the boundary explicitly: Source-of-truth table (orders) -> derived fact (analytics.fct_orders), sync direction stated. This one comment is the contract a reviewer signs.
No re-enforced integrity: order_id is NOT unique in the warehouse: CDC can deliver a row twice on replay, and an analytical model tolerates de-dup downstream. A UNIQUE here would reject good data.
PII held back at the boundary: The raw email never crosses; the sync masks it to customer_hash. Privacy is a property of the boundary, not an afterthought in a later GDPR ticket.
Index for the QUERY PLAN, not the write: ordered_at index serves the dashboard's time-range scans. The OLTP side stays lean; the analytical index lives only in the warehouse.

Rollback touches only the warehouse: DROP the fact table and its index -- the OLTP orders schema is never named in the reversal. That is the proof the boundary held: you can undo analytics without risking transactions.
The reversal condition: A concrete trigger (>0.5% row divergence for 30 min) -- not 'if it feels wrong'. Eventual consistency means you define how much drift is a bug.

storyboard.say: It starts at the checkout app, which commits an ACID write into the Orders database — the operational store that must stay correct under load.
A change-data-capture pipeline tails the OLTP change stream, picking up every committed row without touching the live tables.
The sync loads that data one direction only into the warehouse — a denormalized, eventually-consistent copy built for questions, not transactions.
This is the boundary contract: truth flows source to warehouse and the warehouse NEVER writes back, so analytics can never corrupt operational truth.
On the read side, the BI dashboard queries only the warehouse, keeping every heavy analytical scan far from the checkout path.
The failure path: an analyst runs one innocent full scan straight against the OLTP store, locking rows until checkout latency spikes to nine seconds.
The lesson: a missing boundary let analytics take down the transactional system — enforce the one-way seam and the outage disappears.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.title: Deduplicate CDC soft-duplicates in the analytics warehouse to compute true revenue per customer
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.summary: Write one query the learner runs in the browser that dedupes replayed CDC rows in a warehouse fact table (no unique constraint) down to the latest-loaded row per order, then sums completed-order revenue per customer.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.starter:
-- Boundary: OLTP orders (source of truth) -> analytics.fct_orders (warehouse).
-- The warehouse has NO UNIQUE constraint on order_id, so CDC replays can land the
-- SAME order_id more than once. Each reload gets a fresh loaded_at. The row with the
-- greatest loaded_at is the current truth; older rows are stale soft-duplicates.
-- (This in-memory SQLite table stands in for analytics.fct_orders.)

CREATE TABLE fct_orders (
  order_id      INTEGER,   -- NOT unique: soft-duplicate tolerant
  customer_hash TEXT,
  total_cents   INTEGER,
  status        TEXT,
  ordered_at    TEXT,
  loaded_at     TEXT       -- later load = newer snapshot of that order_id
);

INSERT INTO fct_orders (order_id, customer_hash, total_cents, status, ordered_at, loaded_at) VALUES
  -- order 101: first loaded as 'pending', CDC replay later corrects it to 'completed' + new total
  (101, 'c_ada',  2000, 'pending',   '2024-01-02', '2024-01-02T06:00:00Z'),
  (101, 'c_ada',  2500, 'completed', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03T06:00:00Z'),
  -- order 102: clean single load, completed
  (102, 'c_ada',  4000, 'completed', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-02T06:05:00Z'),
  -- order 103: replayed twice; final snapshot is 'refunded' (must NOT count)
  (103, 'c_bob',  9000, 'completed', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-02T06:10:00Z'),
  (103, 'c_bob',  9000, 'refunded',  '2024-01-02', '2024-01-04T06:10:00Z'),
  -- order 104: bob, completed, single load

observability-incidents.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) database incident and write Section 1 of the packet: the incident framed against an SLO, the three signals you would inspect (a metric, a log/trace, a query plan), and the one observability gap that would have caught it earlier — then attach a rollback trigger.

A reviewer can replay your diagnosis from the signals alone, without you narrating.
observability-incidents.unlock: Your frame names an SLO breach (not a vibe), three real signals across layers (metric · log/trace · query plan), the observability gap, and a rollback trigger.
observability-incidents.doNotClaim: Do not claim you "observed" an incident if your evidence is one dashboard screenshot of CPU. CPU is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Observability means a metric points you, a log/trace explains, and a query plan confirms WHY the database did the slow thing. One number is monitoring; the three-layer trail is observability.

observability-incidents.text: 2:14 a.m.: checkout p99 jumps from 200ms to 9s, the orders table is fine on CPU, and three engineers are arguing about adding read replicas — until the on-call pulls one slow-query log line, runs EXPLAIN, and sees last night's migration silently dropped the index a seq-scan now eats. The fix is a rollback, not replicas. The difference was a signal trail, not a hunch.

This synthesis lesson connects everything earlier in the course — schema, constraints, indexes, migrations, transactions, query plans — to the moment they fail in production at 2 a.m. Observability is how a data model proves it still preserves truth under change and load: metrics point, logs and traces explain, and the query plan confirms the cause inside the database itself.

observability-incidents.prompt: Checkout latency spiked right after a deploy. The dashboard shows database CPU at 95%. Your teammate says "the DB is overloaded, add a replica." Before you agree — what is wrong with that diagnosis? Answer before reading on.
observability-incidents.reveal: High CPU is the symptom, not the cause — and replicas can make it worse if the real issue is a single bad plan. The migration in that deploy may have dropped an index, so a query that was an index seek is now a sequential scan burning CPU on every row. A replica just runs the same seq-scan on more machines. The actual evidence chain is: metric (p99 + CPU) points you, the slow-query log names the statement, and EXPLAIN shows "Seq Scan on orders" where you expected "Index Scan". CPU told you WHERE to look; only the query plan tells you WHY — and the fix is to restore the index, not the hardware.

observability-incidents.intro: Tracing the incident from metric to query plan. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
observability-incidents.code:
-- 1. METRIC: which statements regressed since the deploy? (pg_stat_statements)
SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;
--   top row: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1  mean=842ms (was 3ms)

-- 2. LOG/TRACE: confirm it on the live slow-query log + a trace span
--   log_min_duration_statement = 200ms  ->  orders read tagged on the checkout span

-- 3. QUERY PLAN: ask the engine WHY it is slow
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4815162342;
--   Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0..98214 rows=1 width=240)
--     Filter: (customer_id = 4815162342)   Rows Removed by Filter: 8402911
--   Planning Time: 0.1ms   Execution Time: 841.7ms

-- 4. ROOT CAUSE: the index the planner wanted is gone
SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname = 'idx_orders_customer';
--   (0 rows)  -- last night's migration dropped it
steps: Metric layer — find the regressed statement: pg_stat_statements ranks by mean_exec_time. The orders read jumped from 3ms to 842ms — that is your SLO breach, attributed to one query, not 'the DB is slow'.

Log/trace layer — confirm it is real and live: log_min_duration_statement surfaces it in the live log; the trace span ties it to the checkout request. Now you know it is THIS statement on THIS path, not a coincidence.

Query-plan layer — ask the engine WHY: EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the layer monitoring cannot give you. 'Seq Scan' with 8.4M rows removed by filter is the smoking gun: the planner has no index to seek, so it reads the whole table.

Root cause — name the change that did it: The index idx_orders_customer is gone. Cross-reference the migration: last night's deploy dropped it. Now you have metric → log → plan → cause, a chain a reviewer can replay.

observability-incidents.title: Observability is a three-layer evidence trail: metric points, log/trace explains, query plan confirms

The invariant: every claim traces to evidence across three layers — a metric anchored to an SLO, a log or trace that names the failing work, and a query plan that confirms why the engine did it. Missing a layer means you are guessing.

storyboard.say: 2:14 a.m.: checkout's p99 blows past its SLO, from 200ms to 9 seconds. That breach is where diagnosis starts.
The SLO breach fires an alert into the metric layer, which anchors the pain to a number instead of a hunch.
The metric only says slow, not why. It points down to the log and trace layer, naming one slow statement.
The on-call pulls that one slow-query log line and runs EXPLAIN against it, dropping into the query-plan layer.
The plan confirms WHY: last night's migration dropped an index, so the engine is now eating a full seq-scan.
Root cause named, the rollback trigger is met, so the migration reverts instead of engineers guessing at read replicas.
The same cause exposes the instrumentation gap, an alert we should have had, so the next silent index drop screams early.
The invariant: every claim traces to evidence across three layers, metric points, log explains, plan confirms. Miss one and you are guessing.

observability-incidents.text: Standards grounding: SWEBOK V4 and ACM/IEEE CS2023 both treat operability and evidence-based diagnosis as core software-engineering competencies, and ABET Computing Outcomes require the ability to analyze a problem and identify solutions using evidence. The senior tell in a database incident is the same in all three: a claim about the cause that traces to a query plan, not to a guess about hardware. "Add a replica" without an EXPLAIN is a campaign; "Seq Scan on orders, index dropped by migration 0142" is a diagnosis a reviewer will sign.

observability-incidents.question: Reviewer challenge: an engineer says "checkout was slow, so I added two read replicas and it recovered." What is the strongest evidence that this was a real diagnosis and not a lucky patch?
options: A screenshot showing database CPU dropped after the replicas came online.

A signal trail: pg_stat_statements naming the regressed query, an EXPLAIN showing a Seq Scan from a dropped index, and the migration diff that dropped it — with the rollback that restored the index seek.
A note that latency returned to normal within fifteen minutes of the change.
A statement that the team agreed replicas were the standard fix for high CPU.
observability-incidents.explanation: Only option 2 is observability: a metric attributes the regression to one statement, a query plan confirms WHY (Seq Scan, no index), and the migration diff names the change to reverse. CPU dropping (1) and latency recovering (3) are correlations — replicas can mask a Seq Scan without fixing it, and the index is still gone for the next deploy. Team convention (4) is not evidence at all. The reviewer trusts the trail, not the recovery.

observability-incidents.title: Find the regressed query and confirm its missing index
observability-incidents.summary: Join a query-stats table against the index catalog to surface statements that regressed after a deploy AND have no index on their filter column — the exact triage move from the lesson — running it in the browser against an in-memory SQLite database.
observability-incidents.starter:
-- Incident triage: a deploy at 14:00 made the app slow.
-- You have two observability tables captured from the database.

-- query_stats: one row per statement the DB executed a lot.
--   filter_column = the column the statement filters on (like pg_stat_statements normalized text)
--   mean_ms_before / mean_ms_after = mean execution time before vs after the deploy
CREATE TABLE query_stats (
  statement       TEXT NOT NULL,
  table_name      TEXT NOT NULL,
  filter_column   TEXT NOT NULL,
  calls           INTEGER NOT NULL,
  mean_ms_before  REAL NOT NULL,
  mean_ms_after   REAL NOT NULL
);

-- indexes: the index catalog AFTER the deploy (which indexes still exist).
CREATE TABLE indexes (
  table_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  indexed_column TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO query_stats (statement, table_name, filter_column, calls, mean_ms_before, mean_ms_after) VALUES
  ('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1',   'orders',   'customer_id',  90000, 3.0,   842.0),
  ('SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE token = $1',       'sessions', 'token',        50000, 2.5,   2.7),
  ('SELECT * FROM shipments WHERE order_id = $1',    'shipments','order_id',     12000, 4.0,   611.0),
  ('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1',           'users',    'email',        8000,  1.8,   1.9),
  ('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = $1',   'invoices', 'account_id',   3000,  5.0,   9.0);

-- indexes remaining after the deploy (customer_id and order_id indexes were dropped):
INSERT INTO indexes (table_name, indexed_column) VALUES
  ('sessions', 'token'),
  ('users',    'email'),
  ('invoices', 'account_id');

-- Report every statement that REGRESSED after the deploy
-- (mean_ms_after is at least 10x mean_ms_before) AND whose filter_column
-- has NO matching index in the `indexes` catalog for its table.
-- Return columns: table_name, filter_column, mean_ms_after
-- Order by mean_ms_after descending.

observability-incidents.symptom: After a migration, writes to orders intermittently hang for seconds and some checkout transactions time out — but EXPLAIN on the SELECT looks fine and CPU is normal. The metric layer alone says nothing useful.
observability-incidents.task: The symptom is lock contention, not a slow plan — so the right signal is the LOCK layer, not pg_stat_statements. Name the observability signal that exposes it and the safer migration shape. Keep the repaired failure case as a regression check so the defect cannot silently return.
observability-incidents.fix: Inspect pg_locks / pg_stat_activity (wait_event_type = 'Lock'): the long transaction holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on orders for the whole rewrite, blocking every concurrent write until COMMIT. That is the signal a CPU/latency dashboard hides. The fix is to stop holding one giant lock: add the column with a cheap default, backfill risk_score in batched transactions outside the migration, and build the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so it does not lock writes. Same end state, no peak-hour ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — and the rollback trigger watches lock-wait time, not just latency.

observability-incidents.intro: Prove your incident packet is observable — no vibes:
items: Every claim about the cause traces to a specific signal: name the metric (which query/SLO), the log or trace line, and the query plan. If any layer is missing, you are still guessing.

Your rollback trigger is a concrete threshold a machine could evaluate (p99 > Xs for N min, lock-wait > Ys), not 'roll back if it feels bad'.
Identify the one instrumentation gap that would have caught this earlier (a plan-regression alert, a lock-wait alert, a slow-query threshold) and add it to the packet.

integration-mini-project.text: Friday, 5 p.m.: a product manager needs orders filterable by status, the migration that adds the index has been running for nine minutes holding a lock on the live orders table, and nobody wrote a way back. This lesson is the packet that turns that scene into a controlled, reversible change.

Everything Course 04 taught — schema, constraints, indexes, migrations, transactions, query plans, privacy, backups, data quality — was a single skill rehearsed alone. Production never sends them one at a time; this lesson welds them into one artifact that preserves truth under change, load, and bad input.

integration-mini-project.prompt: Your migration adds a NOT NULL status column to a 40M-row orders table and an index to make it queryable. What is the most likely thing to break in production — and what would prove it before you ship? Answer before reading on.
integration-mini-project.reveal: The NOT NULL is the trap, not the index. Adding a NOT NULL column with no default rewrites or rejects every existing row, and on Postgres an unbatched CREATE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY) takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that freezes reads and writes for the whole build. The proof is a dry-run on a production-sized copy that surfaces the lock wait and the constraint violation BEFORE the real run — exactly the autopsy the packet forces you to write down.

integration-mini-project.intro: Writing the packet's proof, one statement at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: Add nullable, inside a transaction: Migrations · transactions. Adding the column nullable first avoids the full-table rewrite a NOT-NULL-with-no-default would trigger. BEGIN makes the whole change atomic — it all lands or none of it does.
Backfill before you constrain: Data quality. You cannot demand NOT NULL while old rows are null. Backfill every existing row to a real value first — the order matters.
The constraint that protects truth: Constraints. SET NOT NULL is the invariant: from now on no order can exist without a status. This is the line a reviewer checks first.
The new query path, no lock: Indexes. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that freezes a live table — the difference between a 9-minute outage and zero downtime.

Prove the plan changed: Query plans. EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after is the evidence: Seq Scan over 40M rows at 1180 ms becomes an Index Scan at 6 ms. Without this, 'I added an index' is a claim, not a proof.

The rollback — the reverse path: The packet is only reversible if you wrote and ran the way back. DROP INDEX then DROP COLUMN returns the schema to its exact prior state — a two-way door, not a blind leap.

storyboard.say: Before touching the live orders table, take a snapshot. That backup is the way back nobody wrote at 5 p.m. on Friday.
The change runs inside one transaction, so nothing partial ever lands. A privacy boundary bounds what data the migration can even see.
First proof: check the constraint that protects truth. This is the decision point that sends us forward or into repair.
On pass, compare the query plan before and after to prove the index actually improved how orders filter by status.
Third proof: a data-quality check that row counts match. Only then does the transaction commit as the source of truth.
If the constraint is violated, run the rollback script instead of committing broken schema onto the live table.
The rollback restores from the snapshot, returning the schema to its prior state. The change is fully reversible.
The lesson: welded together, backups, transactions, constraints, plans, and quality checks turn a risky migration into a controlled, reversible change.

integration-mini-project.text: Standards grounding (SWEBOK V4 Software Configuration Management and Maintenance): the senior tell on a migration is not that it works — it's that the rollback was tested before the forward run shipped. (There is no SWEBOK 'data management' KA; controlled/reversible change belongs to Configuration Management.) Reviewers trust the engineer who can answer 'what happens when this is wrong at 2 a.m.?' with a script, not a shrug. Reversibility is the whole game; a one-way migration with no proven back path is an outage waiting for a trigger.

integration-mini-project.question: Reviewer challenge: you claim your migration packet is production-ready. Which single piece of evidence proves it is reversible and measured — not just a happy-path run?
options: The migration ran without an error on your local machine.

A backfill-then-SET-NOT-NULL forward block, an EXPLAIN ANALYZE before/after showing Seq Scan → Index Scan, AND a rollback script you executed on a production-sized copy to return the schema to its prior state.
The new column has a descriptive name and a comment.
You took a database backup before starting, so you could restore the whole database if needed.
integration-mini-project.explanation: Only option 2 proves both axes the packet exists to defend: measured (EXPLAIN before/after is evidence the index changed the plan, not a guess) and reversible (an executed rollback returns the schema to its exact prior state — a two-way door). A clean local run (1) tests nothing about production load or constraints; a name (3) is cosmetics; a full-database backup (4) is a blunt last resort, not a surgical, tested rollback — restoring 40M rows to undo one column is the failure this packet replaces.

The same packet pattern transfers to any high-stakes change with a hidden blast radius: a data-pipeline cutover, a privacy-driven column drop under GDPR, a tenant-isolation migration in a multi-tenant schema — each one stays invariant on 'preserve truth, prove the plan, keep a tested way back,' and changes only in which constraint protects truth and what the rollback restores. This is your capstone evidence: not 'I understand data modeling,' but 'here is a migration I framed, constrained, indexed, measured, and proved reversible — read it, then run it.' Carry schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md straight into the database capstone; the capstone reuses this exact artifact and proof. You don't just describe a safe migration now. You can ship one and take it back.

database-capstone.text: Friday, 6 p.m.: a migration to add a unique index on (org_id, email) has been running for nine minutes, it just took an exclusive lock on the users table, every signup is timing out — and nobody wrote the rollback. The engineer who shipped a packet with a tested down-script is calm; the one who shipped a bare ALTER is on the phone with the VP.

This is the synthesis lesson of Databases and Data Modeling: every prior skill — schema design, constraints, indexes, transactions, migrations, query plans, privacy, backups, data quality — converges on one decision. The win is not understanding any one of them; it is assembling them into a packet that preserves truth under change, load, and bad input.

database-capstone.prompt: "The migration ran in staging with no errors, so it is safe to deploy." Before you ship it — what is the load-bearing thing that sentence quietly skips? Answer before reading on.
database-capstone.reveal: Two things, and both are about reversibility under real conditions. Staging has no production data volume, so a CREATE INDEX that returned instantly on 200 rows can hold an exclusive lock for minutes on 40M rows — the same DDL, a different blast radius. And "no errors forward" says nothing about backward: a migration without a tested down-script is an irreversible change wearing a reversible costume. The capstone bar is not "it ran" — it is "it ran, I can prove the new query path is faster, and I can put it back."

database-capstone.intro: The migration + rollback, one statement at a time. Trace the schema, query grain, invariant, and observable result before editing the SQL lab.
steps: Build the index CONCURRENTLY: The naive path — ALTER TABLE ... ADD UNIQUE — takes an exclusive lock and blocks every write for the build. CONCURRENTLY trades a longer build for zero downtime on a 40M-row table. This is the index + transaction skill doing the real work.

Promote index → constraint: USING INDEX adopts the already-built index instead of rebuilding it, so the constraint add is near-instant. This is where the data model's invariant becomes an enforced constraint the database guarantees.

Verify the invariant holds NOW: Run BEFORE promoting in a dry run: if this returns any row, real duplicate data already violates the constraint and the ADD will fail. Data quality is checked, not assumed.

The rollback — the part most people skip: DROP CONSTRAINT then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY returns the schema to its exact prior state. IF EXISTS makes the down-script idempotent so a half-applied migration can be retried. This is the line that turns a one-way door into a two-way door.

storyboard.say: Start with the data model. Every change begins here, and from it we derive the one integrity invariant we can never violate.
The constraint must hold across the whole change. Unique on org_id and email is the truth the migration has to preserve, not break.
The migration applies DDL to Postgres. This is the trigger: the schema is moving forward while every signup is still hitting the table.
The naive path is the trap. A plain unique index takes an exclusive lock, and nine minutes in, every signup times out in a lock storm.
The repair is CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY plus a backfill, building the index without freezing writes. The safe path skips the storm entirely.
The index enables the query plan. Compare plans before and after: that's your proof the new path is actually used, not just present.
Reversibility is the other half. The migration is paired with a tested rollback that restores the prior schema; the backup and PITR catch what rollback can't.
The insight: invariant plus reversibility plus proof, never one alone. That packet is what survives change, load, and bad input.

database-capstone.question: Reviewer challenge: which single piece of evidence best proves this migration packet is capstone-ready, not just understood?
options: The forward DDL ran without errors in staging.
A round-trip transcript: UP then DOWN against a scratch clone leaves a byte-identical schema, plus an EXPLAIN showing the new query path is an index scan.
A paragraph explaining why unique constraints matter.
The migration is short and reads cleanly.
database-capstone.explanation: Capstone readiness is reversibility + proof, not forward success. Option 2 demonstrates the rollback actually restores the prior state (two-way door) AND that the new index changed the query plan (the goal was met). Forward-only success (1), prose (3), and brevity (4) all leave the dangerous question — can you put it back, and did it work — unanswered.

database-capstone.title: Find rows that would violate a per-org, case-insensitive email uniqueness invariant before adding the constraint
database-capstone.summary: Write the verification query from a real migration — group the users table by org and lowercased email to surface every collision that would block a new UNIQUE (org_id, lower(email)) constraint — and run it in the browser.
database-capstone.starter:
-- Migration capstone: you are about to add a per-org unique invariant on
--   UNIQUE (org_id, lower(email))
-- so that within one org, emails are unique case-insensitively.
-- Before promoting the index into a constraint, you MUST prove no existing
-- data violates it. Write the "verify" query that lists each colliding group.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  email   TEXT    NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO users (id, org_id, email) VALUES
  (1, 10, 'ada@acme.io'),
  (2, 10, 'grace@acme.io'),
  (3, 10, 'ADA@acme.io'),     -- collides with id 1 (same org, same email ignoring case)
  (4, 20, 'ada@acme.io'),     -- different org, so NOT a collision with id 1
  (5, 20, 'lin@beta.dev'),
  (6, 20, 'Lin@beta.dev'),    -- collides with id 5
  (7, 20, 'lin@BETA.dev'),    -- also collides with id 5
  (8, 30, 'sole@gamma.co');

-- TODO: Return one row per violating group.
-- Columns (in this order and with these names):
--   org_id, email_key, dup_count
-- where email_key is the lowercased email, and dup_count is how many rows
-- share that (org_id, email_key). Only include groups with more than one row.
-- Order by org_id, then email_key, so the output is deterministic.
